cards.back: Some alpha particles scattered through large angles, implying a tiny, dense positive nucleus.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why do isotopes often have similar chemical properties?
cards.back: They have the same electron arrangements despite differing neutron numbers.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Define relative molecular mass Mr.
cards.back: Mean mass of a molecule compared with 1/12 of a carbon-12 atom.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is relative isotopic mass compared against?
cards.back: One twelfth of the mass of one carbon-12 atom.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How do you calculate Ar from two isotope abundances?
cards.back: (isotope mass₁×abundance₁ + mass₂×abundance₂) ÷ total abundance.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is Ar of an isotope mixture a weighted mean?
cards.back: More abundant isotopes contribute more to the average mass.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does m/z mean in mass spectrometry?
cards.back: Mass-to-charge ratio; for a singly charged ion it matches the relative ion mass.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What are the four core TOF stages in order?
cards.back: Ionisation → acceleration → ion drift → detection/data analysis.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the purpose of ionisation in TOF?
cards.back: To give sample particles an electrical charge so they can be accelerated and detected.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is formed by electron-impact ionisation of X(g)?
cards.back: X⁺(g), after an electron is removed.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why may electron-impact mass spectra show fragment peaks?
cards.back: Energetic ionisation can break molecules into smaller charged fragments.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What charge is commonly formed by electrospray protonation?
cards.back: A singly charged protonated ion, [M+H]⁺.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can electrospray help analyse large molecules?
cards.back: It is gentler and often causes less fragmentation than electron impact.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens to positive ions in the acceleration stage?
cards.back: An electric field accelerates them, giving ions of equal charge equal kinetic energy.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does equal kinetic energy not mean equal speed?
cards.back: Since Eₖ=½mv², lighter ions have greater speed at equal Eₖ.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which travels faster at equal KE: 63⁺ or 65⁺?
cards.back: The lighter 63⁺ ion.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the purpose of the flight/drift tube?
cards.back: To time how long accelerated ions take to travel a fixed distance.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is a high vacuum used in the drift tube?
cards.back: To reduce collisions between moving ions and gas molecules.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens to an ion's speed while drifting ideally?
cards.back: It remains approximately constant in the field-free drift region.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the relationship between flight time, distance and speed?
cards.back: Flight time t = flight length L ÷ speed v.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How does flight time change as mass increases at fixed KE and charge?
cards.back: It increases; t is proportional to the square root of mass.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens when ions reach a TOF detector?
cards.back: They generate an electrical signal used to record ion arrivals.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does the position of a mass spectrum peak indicate?
cards.back: Its mass-to-charge ratio (m/z).

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does the height/intensity of a mass spectrum peak indicate?
cards.back: Relative abundance of the detected ion.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the base peak in a mass spectrum?
cards.back: The most intense peak; it is assigned 100% relative intensity.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is the base peak not necessarily the molecular ion?
cards.back: A charged fragment can be more abundant than the intact molecular ion.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a molecular-ion peak represent in electron-impact MS?
cards.back: An ion formed from the intact molecule after losing an electron.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why might the electrospray [M+H]⁺ peak differ from molecular mass?
cards.back: It includes the mass of an added proton; m/z is about Mr+1 for 1+ ions.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: For a 36 u ion with a 2+ charge, what is m/z?

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: At fixed voltage, how does a higher ion charge affect kinetic energy?
cards.back: Eₖ=qV; a higher charge gains more kinetic energy.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What simple relation links acceleration voltage and ion energy?
cards.back: Kinetic energy gained = charge × potential difference, Eₖ=qV.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How can elemental identity be suggested by mass spectrometry?
cards.back: Compare isotope peak masses and relative abundances to characteristic isotope patterns.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write the first ionisation equation for magnesium.
cards.back: Mg(g) → Mg⁺(g) + e⁻.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write the second ionisation equation for magnesium.
cards.back: Mg⁺(g) → Mg²⁺(g) + e⁻.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why do successive ionisation energies increase?
cards.back: Each electron is removed from an increasingly positive ion.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a very large successive-IE jump identify?
cards.back: Removal has reached an inner shell; the number removed before it equals outer-shell electrons.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does first IE usually rise across Period 3?
cards.back: Nuclear charge rises; shielding changes little; outer electrons are held more strongly.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is Al first IE lower than Mg first IE?
cards.back: Al loses a higher-energy 3p electron; Mg loses a lower-energy 3s electron.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is S first IE lower than P first IE?
cards.back: Electron repulsion within a paired 3p orbital in S helps one electron escape.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does first IE fall down Group 2?
cards.back: Outer electrons are farther away and more shielded, despite a larger nuclear charge.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How many electrons can an s, p and d subshell hold?

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What are the exceptional electron configurations of chromium and copper?
cards.back: Cr: [Ar]3d⁵4s¹; Cu: [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the configuration of Fe²⁺?
cards.back: [Ar]3d⁶; electrons are removed from 4s before 3d.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the configuration of Fe³⁺?
cards.back: [Ar]3d⁵; after both 4s electrons, one 3d electron is lost.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is Hund's rule when filling degenerate orbitals?
cards.back: Electrons occupy equal-energy orbitals singly before pairing.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the difference between empirical and molecular formula?
cards.back: Empirical: simplest atom ratio. Molecular: actual atoms per molecule.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How should percentages be treated when calculating empirical formula?
cards.back: Assume a 100 g sample; percentage values become gram masses.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What are the three stages of empirical formula calculation?
cards.back: Divide element masses by Ar; divide moles by smallest; find integer ratio.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: If empirical atom ratio is 1:1.5:2.5, what ratio is needed?
cards.back: Multiply by 2 to obtain 2:3:5.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How is molecular formula calculated from empirical formula?
cards.back: Find empirical-formula Mr, divide molecular Mr by it, multiply subscripts.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: With empirical formula CH₂O and molecular Mr 180, what is the molecular formula?
cards.back: C₆H₁₂O₆.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: State the ideal-gas equation.
cards.back: pV = nRT.
accept: pressure x volume = moles x R x temperature

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How many cubic metres are in 1 cm³?
accept: one millionth of a cubic metre

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why must Celsius temperatures be converted for pV=nRT?
cards.back: The absolute temperature is required, in kelvin (K).

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How do you find n from gas pressure, volume and temperature?
cards.back: n=pV/(RT), using SI units.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How do you calculate molar mass of an unknown gas from mass and gas data?
cards.back: First n=pV/(RT), then molar mass M=m/n.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What approximate molar volume is commonly used at RTP?
cards.back: About 24 dm³ mol⁻¹; use pV=nRT if P and T are specified.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How is the limiting reagent identified?
cards.back: Compare moles available divided by their balanced-equation coefficients.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why must a limiting-reagent calculation consider stoichiometry?
cards.back: Equal numbers of moles do not imply reactants are present in required ratios.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How do you convert gas moles into a volume at RTP?
cards.back: Approximately V(dm³)=n×24, when RTP approximation is appropriate.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the formula for percentage yield?
cards.back: 100×actual yield/theoretical yield, using the same units.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why may actual percentage yield be below 100%?
cards.back: Incomplete reaction, side reactions or material lost during recovery.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How is percentage atom economy calculated from a balanced equation?
cards.back: 100 × (coefficient × Mr of desired product) ÷ sum of (coefficient × Mr) for all products.
accept: 100 × (coefficient × Mr of desired product) ÷ sum of (coefficient × Mr) for all products.
Mr of desired product / total Mr products x 100 accounting for coefficients
desired product stoichiometric Mr divided by total product stoichiometric Mr times 100
mass of desired product over total mass of all products times 100

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the difference between atom economy and percentage yield?
cards.back: Atom economy is theoretical atom distribution; yield compares actual and maximum product.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why might industries prefer high atom economy?
cards.back: Less unwanted waste; reduced raw-material, disposal and environmental costs.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Can a reaction have high atom economy but low percentage yield?
cards.back: Yes. Theoretical atom use can be efficient even if little product is recovered.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How are spectator ions identified for an ionic equation?
cards.back: They remain unchanged on both sides of the full ionic equation.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write the net ionic equation for acid–alkali neutralisation.
cards.back: H⁺(aq)+OH⁻(aq)→H₂O(l).

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write the net ionic equation for barium sulfate precipitation.
cards.back: Ba²⁺(aq)+SO₄²⁻(aq)→BaSO₄(s).

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How is x found in salt·xH₂O from heating data?
cards.back: Find moles of anhydrous salt and lost water, then divide water moles by salt moles.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What mass is lost when a hydrated salt releases water?
cards.back: Initial hydrated mass minus final anhydrous mass.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why heat a hydrated solid to constant mass?
cards.back: To provide evidence that the removable water has been driven off.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What number is represented by the Avogadro constant?
cards.back: Number of particles per mole, approximately 6.02×10²³ mol⁻¹.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How do you count ions in a salt using Avogadro's constant?
cards.back: Find moles of salt, multiply by ions per formula unit, then by N_A.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the chemical purpose of an acid–base titration?
cards.back: Use a known concentration and reacting ratio to calculate an unknown concentration.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How are concordant titre values treated?
cards.back: Exclude clear outliers; mean the close repeat titres.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is meant by a titre?
cards.back: The volume delivered from the burette: final reading minus initial.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why are two burette readings included in uncertainty?
cards.back: A titre is a difference; uncertainty arises from both final and initial readings.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How is percentage titre uncertainty found?
cards.back: Absolute titre uncertainty ÷ titre ×100.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why rinse a pipette with the measured solution first?
cards.back: To avoid diluting it with residual water.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why rinse the burette with the solution it will hold?
cards.back: To avoid diluting the titrant with residual water.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is a volumetric flask inverted after filling to the mark?
cards.back: To mix the prepared solution uniformly.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why rinse solution traces from beaker/funnel into the volumetric flask?
cards.back: To transfer the dissolved solute quantitatively.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can distilled water be added to the conical flask during a titration?
cards.back: It changes concentration but not the number of moles being titrated.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How is the meniscus viewed accurately?
cards.back: Read the bottom of the colourless meniscus at eye level.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why use a back titration rather than a direct titration?
cards.back: The sample may be insoluble or react slowly; excess reagent is measured indirectly.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What quantity does a back titration determine directly?
cards.back: Amount of an intentionally excess reagent remaining unreacted.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: State the essential subtraction in a back titration.
cards.back: Initial moles of reagent minus remaining moles = moles that reacted.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why must dilution factors be applied in a back titration?
cards.back: An aliquot represents only a fraction of the total diluted solution.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: A 25 cm³ aliquot came from 250 cm³. What is the factor?
cards.back: 10: total remaining moles = aliquot moles ×10.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why calculate the excess acid before finding sample mass?
cards.back: Only acid consumed reacts with sample; excess acid does not count.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: For CaCO₃+2HCl, how are CaCO₃ moles found?
cards.back: Moles CaCO₃ = moles HCl that reacted ÷2.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the last step after computing analyte mass?
cards.back: Find percentage purity = analyte mass/sample mass ×100.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write chromium's ground-state electron configuration.
cards.back: [Ar]3d⁵4s¹.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write copper's ground-state electron configuration.
cards.back: [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does Cr have one 4s electron rather than two?
cards.back: Its 3d⁵ half-filled subshell is especially favourable.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does Cu have one 4s electron rather than two?
cards.back: Its 3d¹⁰ full subshell is especially favourable.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which element has a half-filled 3d subshell: Cr or Cu?
cards.back: Chromium (Cr).

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the electron configuration of Cr³⁺?
cards.back: [Ar]3d³. Remove the 4s electron first, then two 3d electrons.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the electron configuration of Cu²⁺?
cards.back: [Ar]3d⁹. Remove one 4s electron and then one 3d electron.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the electron configuration of Cu⁺?
cards.back: [Ar]3d¹⁰. Remove copper's 4s¹ electron.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: When transition-metal ions form, which electrons leave first?
cards.back: The 4s electrons are removed before 3d electrons.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is '4s fills first, so 3d empties first' incorrect?
cards.back: 4s generally fills before 3d, but 4s electrons are removed first in these ions.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How does shielding change across Period 3, helping first ionisation energy rise?
cards.back: It remains approximately the same.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which two different causes explain the Period 3 first-IE dips?
cards.back: Mg→Al: higher-energy 3p versus 3s. P→S: extra repulsion from paired 3p electrons.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which two drops interrupt the general rise in first ionisation energy across Period 3?
cards.back: Mg to Al (3p electron) and P to S (3p electron pairing).
accept: Mg to Al (3p electron) and P to S (3p electron pairing).

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: State the complete definition of ionic bonding.
cards.back: Strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in a lattice.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is NaCl not made of separate NaCl molecules?
cards.back: The ions form a giant 3D lattice attracted in all directions.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What charges do Group 1, 2 and 13 elements commonly form?
cards.back: +1, +2 and +3 ions respectively.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What charges do Group 15, 16 and 17 non-metals commonly form?
cards.back: −3, −2 and −1 ions respectively.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Give formulae and charges of sulfate, carbonate and nitrate.
cards.back: SO₄²⁻, CO₃²⁻ and NO₃⁻.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Give formulae and charges of hydroxide and ammonium.
cards.back: OH⁻ and NH₄⁺.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the formula of aluminium sulfate from Al³⁺ and SO₄²⁻?
cards.back: Al₂(SO₄)₃: total charges +6 and −6 balance.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the formula of ammonium carbonate?
cards.back: (NH₄)₂CO₃: two NH₄⁺ balance one CO₃²⁻.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What makes the electrostatic attraction in an ionic solid stronger?
cards.back: Higher ion charges and smaller distances between ion centres.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Define a single covalent bond accurately.
cards.back: One electron pair shared between atoms and attracted to both nuclei.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How many shared pairs are in a double and a triple covalent bond?
cards.back: Two and three shared electron pairs respectively.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a coordinate or dative covalent bond?
cards.back: A shared pair where both electrons originate from one atom.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How is a coordinate bond represented in a diagram?
cards.back: With an arrow pointing from electron-pair donor to acceptor.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How does NH₄⁺ form from NH₃ and H⁺?
cards.back: Nitrogen donates its lone pair to H⁺, making a dative covalent bond.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which species donates the lone pair in NH₃→BF₃?
cards.back: The nitrogen atom in NH₃ donates to electron-deficient boron in BF₃.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: After formation, is a dative bond weaker by definition?
cards.back: No; its origin differs, but it is an ordinary covalent bond once formed.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: State the complete definition of metallic bonding.
cards.back: Attraction between positive metal ions in a lattice and delocalised electrons.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can a metal carry electrical current in the solid state?
cards.back: Mobile delocalised electrons carry charge through the lattice.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why are metals malleable rather than brittle like typical ionic solids?
cards.back: Ion layers can slide while delocalised electrons maintain attraction.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is Mg metallic bonding often stronger than Na?
cards.back: Mg offers greater positive charge and more delocalised electrons; ions are smaller.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Name the four AQA crystal structure types.
cards.back: Ionic, metallic, giant covalent (macromolecular), molecular.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Give one AQA example of a giant covalent crystal.
cards.back: Diamond (or graphite).

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which particles carry electricity in molten NaCl?
cards.back: Mobile Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, not free electrons.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does solid NaCl not conduct electricity?
cards.back: Its ions are fixed within the giant ionic lattice.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can aqueous NaCl solution conduct electricity?
cards.back: Dissolved Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions can move and carry charge.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is an ionic lattice's melting point usually high?
cards.back: Strong attractions among many oppositely charged ions need much energy to overcome.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How many covalent bonds does each carbon make in diamond?
cards.back: Four, in a three-dimensional tetrahedral network.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does diamond have an extremely high melting point?
cards.back: Many strong covalent C–C bonds throughout the giant lattice must be broken.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does diamond not conduct electricity?
cards.back: No mobile ions or delocalised electrons are available.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does graphite's bonding look like?
cards.back: Each C forms three covalent bonds in layers of hexagonal rings; one electron is delocalised.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can graphite conduct along its layers?
cards.back: Delocalised electrons move through the layers.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can graphite's layers slide past one another?
cards.back: Only weak attractions act between layers.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does graphite have a high melting point despite weak interlayer attractions?
cards.back: Heating to melt requires disrupting the strong covalent networks within layers.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What kind of crystal is solid iodine I₂?
cards.back: Molecular: discrete I₂ molecules with weak intermolecular attractions.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which interactions are overcome when solid iodine sublimes?
cards.back: Intermolecular van der Waals' forces, not the I–I covalent bond.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What kind of solid is ice?
cards.back: A molecular solid with extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonding.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is liquid water denser than ice?
cards.back: Ice has an open hydrogen-bonded lattice; melting lets molecules pack closer.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is broken or weakened when ice melts?
cards.back: Some intermolecular hydrogen bonds, not the O–H covalent bonds.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does a change of state absorb or release energy?
cards.back: Intermolecular attractions or other bonding interactions are overcome or formed.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which type of bonding causes high melting points in magnesium?
cards.back: Metallic electrostatic attractions involving positive ions and delocalised electrons.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why are simple molecular solids usually low-melting?
cards.back: Relatively weak intermolecular forces, not the internal covalent bonds, are overcome.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How can conductivity and melting data help identify an unknown crystal?
cards.back: Combine mobile charge carriers and strength/type of interactions to infer structure.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What determines molecular geometry by VSEPR?
cards.back: Electron domains repel and occupy positions as far apart as possible.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Rank lone–lone, lone–bond and bond–bond pair repulsion.
cards.back: Lone–lone > lone–bond > bond–bond.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does a lone pair make neighbouring bond angles smaller?
cards.back: Its electron density repels bonding regions more strongly.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What shape and angle result from two electron domains and no lone pairs?
cards.back: Linear, 180° (e.g. BeCl₂, CO₂).

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What shape and angle result from three bonding domains?
cards.back: Trigonal planar, 120° (e.g. BF₃).

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What shape is SO₂ with two bonding regions and one lone pair?
cards.back: Bent, angle slightly less than 120°.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What shape and angle has CH₄?
cards.back: Tetrahedral, 109.5°, with four bonding domains.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What shape and approximate angle has NH₃?
cards.back: Trigonal pyramidal, about 107°; 3 bonds + 1 lone pair.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What shape and approximate angle has H₂O?
cards.back: Bent, about 104.5°; 2 bonds + 2 lone pairs.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the molecular shape of NH₄⁺?
cards.back: Tetrahedral.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the molecular shape of H₃O⁺?
cards.back: Trigonal pyramidal.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does NH₃ have a smaller bond angle than CH₄?
cards.back: NH₃ has one lone pair, which repels bond pairs more strongly.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does H₂O have a smaller angle than NH₃?
cards.back: H₂O has two lone pairs, which increase repulsion of bonding regions.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the molecular shape of gaseous PCl₅?
cards.back: Trigonal bipyramidal.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What shape does SF₄ have with 5 electron domains?
cards.back: Seesaw: 4 bonding regions and 1 lone pair, from trigonal bipyramidal.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What shape does ClF₃ have with 5 electron domains?
cards.back: T-shaped: 3 bonding regions and 2 lone pairs.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What shape is XeF₂ despite having 3 lone pairs?
cards.back: Linear: 2 bonding regions and 3 equatorial lone pairs.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the molecular shape of SF₆?
cards.back: Octahedral.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What shape does BrF₅ have?
cards.back: Square pyramidal: 5 bonding regions and 1 lone pair.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the molecular shape of XeF₄?
cards.back: Square planar.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Does a double bond count as one or two electron domains in VSEPR?
cards.back: One region of electron density, although it contains two shared pairs.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the safest method for an unfamiliar VSEPR molecule?
cards.back: Draw Lewis structure; count electron domains and lone pairs; assign geometry and angle.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Define electronegativity.
cards.back: Ability of an atom to attract the shared electron pair in a covalent bond.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What do δ+ and δ− mean on a polar bond?
cards.back: Partial positive and partial negative charges caused by uneven electron sharing.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is an H–Cl bond polar?
cards.back: Cl is more electronegative and draws the shared electron pair toward itself.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is CO₂ overall non-polar despite two polar C=O bonds?
cards.back: Its linear, symmetrical bond dipoles cancel.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is BF₃ overall non-polar despite polar B–F bonds?
cards.back: Three identical bond dipoles cancel in a symmetrical trigonal planar arrangement.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is CCl₄ overall non-polar despite polar C–Cl bonds?
cards.back: The tetrahedrally arranged bond dipoles cancel.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is H₂O polar?
cards.back: Its bent geometry means the polar O–H bond dipoles do not cancel.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How can a molecule have polar bonds but no permanent dipole?
cards.back: Its geometry may make equal bond dipoles cancel vectorially.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which three intermolecular forces are in AQA 3.1.3.7?
cards.back: van der Waals' (induced dipole–dipole) forces, permanent dipole–dipole and hydrogen bonding.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Do all atoms and molecules have van der Waals' (induced dipole–dipole) forces?
cards.back: Yes: instantaneous fluctuations create temporary induced dipoles.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What causes induced dipole–dipole (van der Waals') attraction?
cards.back: Temporary electron-density fluctuations induce dipoles in neighbouring particles.
accept: Temporary electron-density fluctuations induce dipoles in neighbouring particles.
instantaneous dipoles induce dipoles in neighbouring molecules

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why do van der Waals' forces generally increase for larger molecules?
cards.back: More electrons and greater polarizability make induced dipoles stronger.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can straight-chain molecules boil above more branched isomers?
cards.back: Greater surface contact generally strengthens van der Waals' forces.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: When do permanent dipole–dipole forces occur?
cards.back: Between neighbouring polar molecules with permanent dipoles.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What atoms must H be bonded to for strong usual hydrogen bonding?
cards.back: Nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What other feature is essential for intermolecular hydrogen bonding?
cards.back: A nearby lone pair on N, O or F acts as an electron-pair acceptor site.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Does HCl form conventional hydrogen bonds between HCl molecules?
cards.back: No; usual hydrogen bonding in this syllabus needs H bonded to N, O or F.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does water have unusually high boiling point for its mass?
cards.back: An extensive hydrogen-bond network needs substantial energy to overcome.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why do NH₃, H₂O and HF have anomalous boiling points?
cards.back: They can form intermolecular hydrogen bonds.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens to covalent O–H bonds when water boils?
cards.back: They stay intact; intermolecular hydrogen bonds are overcome instead.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is ice less dense than liquid water?
cards.back: Its hydrogen bonds create an open tetrahedral network with more empty space.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How many hydrogen bonds can one water molecule form in ideal ice?
cards.back: Four: two via its O–H hydrogens and two via lone-pair acceptor sites.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does I₂ boil at a higher temperature than Cl₂?
cards.back: I₂ has more electrons; stronger van der Waals' (induced dipole–dipole) forces.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How should a boiling-point comparison be explained fully?
cards.back: Identify the forces, compare their strength and state the energy needed to overcome them.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Are intermolecular forces and covalent bonds the same?
cards.back: No: intermolecular forces attract molecules; covalent bonds join atoms within molecules.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is an enthalpy change?
cards.back: Heat energy change measured at constant pressure.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does negative ΔH mean?
cards.back: Exothermic: heat is released to the surroundings.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does positive ΔH mean?
cards.back: Endothermic: heat is absorbed from the surroundings.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Where do products lie on an exothermic enthalpy profile?
cards.back: Lower in enthalpy than the reactants.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Where do products lie on an endothermic enthalpy profile?
cards.back: Higher in enthalpy than the reactants.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Does an exothermic reaction necessarily have zero activation energy?
cards.back: No; activation energy is a barrier, not the reaction's enthalpy change.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Does a catalyst change a reaction's ΔH?
cards.back: No; it changes activation energy, not the initial/final enthalpy difference.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What pressure counts as standard pressure for AQA ΔH°?
cards.back: 100 kPa.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What conditions must standard enthalpy values use?
cards.back: 100 kPa, a stated temperature and specified standard states.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Define standard enthalpy of formation precisely.
cards.back: ΔH when 1 mol of compound forms from elements in standard states under standard conditions.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the ΔfH° of an element in its standard state?
cards.back: Zero, by definition.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Is ΔfH° of gaseous oxygen atoms O(g) zero?
cards.back: No; oxygen's standard state is O₂(g).

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Give a formation equation for magnesium oxide.
cards.back: Mg(s)+½O₂(g)→MgO(s).

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Give the standard formation equation of liquid water.
cards.back: H₂(g)+½O₂(g)→H₂O(l).

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Define standard enthalpy of combustion.
cards.back: ΔH when 1 mol of substance burns completely in O₂ under standard conditions/states.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the standard combustion equation for methane?
cards.back: CH₄(g)+2O₂(g)→CO₂(g)+2H₂O(l).

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why must states be shown in an enthalpy equation?
cards.back: Changing a substance's physical state changes the enthalpy value.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens to ΔH if a whole reaction equation is doubled?
cards.back: ΔH for the doubled equation also doubles.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens to ΔH if a reaction is reversed?
cards.back: The enthalpy sign reverses.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What equation relates heat, mass, specific heat capacity and temperature rise?
cards.back: q=mcΔT with q in J, m in g, c in J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How is ΔT calculated from initial and final temperatures?
cards.back: ΔT=T_final−T_initial; changes in °C and K are numerically equal.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: When liquid density is 1 g cm⁻³, how does mass relate to volume?
cards.back: Solution mass in grams approximately equals its volume in cm³.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: In a solution calorimeter, what mass usually goes in q=mcΔT?
cards.back: Mass of the solution that changes temperature, not only the solute.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How do you convert calorimetry q from J into kJ?
cards.back: Divide by 1000.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How do you calculate reaction molar ΔH using solution q?
cards.back: ΔH=−q_solution(kJ)/moles of reaction, with sign chosen correctly.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is ΔH negative if the solution warms?
cards.back: The solution gains heat, so the reaction has released it.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is ΔH positive if the solution cools?
cards.back: The solution loses heat; the reaction absorbs heat from surroundings.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why must a reaction mole ratio be checked before finding molar ΔH?
cards.back: The enthalpy is defined per mole of reaction as written; reactants may have unequal ratios.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: For 25 cm³ 1 M HCl plus 25 cm³ 1 M NaOH, how many mol water form?
cards.back: 0.025 mol, assuming complete 1:1 neutralisation.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the purpose of a calorimeter's insulation?
cards.back: To reduce heat transfer between system and external surroundings.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens to the measured magnitude of exothermic ΔH if heat escapes?
cards.back: The temperature rise is too small; calculated ΔH is less negative.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens when an endothermic experiment gains external heat?
cards.back: Temperature fall is too small; measured ΔH is underestimated in magnitude.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why might a fuel combustion calorimetry estimate be too weak?
cards.back: Some heat escapes or warms apparatus, so measured water rise is too small.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can incomplete combustion affect fuel calorimetry?
cards.back: Not all fuel undergoes the stated complete combustion reaction.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does extrapolating a temperature–time graph estimate?
cards.back: Corrected temperature at the mixing/reaction time, reducing heat-exchange error.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Name one measurement uncertainty in calorimetry.
cards.back: Temperature measurement.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Does AQA require the specific heat capacity of water from memory?
cards.back: No; the value is supplied when needed.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: State Hess's law.
cards.back: Overall enthalpy change is independent of pathway if start/end states match.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the formation-enthalpy calculation for ΔH°reaction?
cards.back: Sum of product ΔfH° values minus sum of reactant ΔfH° values.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the combustion-enthalpy Hess calculation?
cards.back: Sum combustion enthalpies of reactants minus those of products.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why do equation coefficients matter in Hess calculations?
cards.back: Multiply each substance's molar enthalpy by its stoichiometric coefficient.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens to a Hess enthalpy when an equation is reversed?
cards.back: Change the sign.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens to a Hess enthalpy when the equation is halved?
cards.back: Halve the ΔH value.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is the ΔfH° of H₂(g) zero?
cards.back: Hydrogen gas is elemental hydrogen in its standard state.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What common starting point is used in a formation-enthalpy Hess cycle?
cards.back: The constituent elements in their standard states.
accept: The constituent elements in their standard states.
the elements in their standard states

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: In a combustion cycle, what common products can both pathways reach?
cards.back: Complete combustion products, typically CO₂(g) and H₂O(l).

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can Hess's law calculate a reaction not measured directly?
cards.back: A sum of accessible reactions can have the same overall initial and final states.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: If anhydrous salt → solution has ΔH₁ and hydrated salt → solution has ΔH₂, what is ΔH for anhydrous → hydrated salt?
cards.back: ΔH₁ − ΔH₂ (for matching amounts and states).
accept: ΔH₁ − ΔH₂ (for matching amounts and states).

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How can enthalpies of solution determine hydration of a salt?
cards.back: Construct paths to the same aqueous final state; subtract the two dissolution ΔHs.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Define mean bond enthalpy.
cards.back: Average enthalpy change to break one mole of a specified covalent bond in gaseous molecules.
accept: Average enthalpy change to break one mole of a specified covalent bond in gaseous molecules.
average enthalpy needed to break one mole of a specified bond in gaseous molecules
average energy to break one mole of a covalent bond in gaseous molecules

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the general bond-enthalpy estimate for reaction ΔH?
cards.back: Sum of energies for bonds broken − sum of energies for bonds formed.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the sign of bond breaking?
cards.back: Positive (endothermic): energy is required.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the sign of bond formation?
cards.back: Negative contribution (exothermic): energy is released.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why must you count all bonds in the balanced equation?
cards.back: Coefficients determine the number of each bond broken and formed.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Are mean bond enthalpies exact for a specific compound?
cards.back: No; they are averages across different molecular environments.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can mean bond-enthalpy ΔH differ from standard experimental ΔH?
cards.back: Mean gas-phase energies are approximate and actual substances may have other states.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is liquid water a problem if only gas-phase mean bonds are used?
cards.back: Condensation/phase enthalpy is omitted unless accounted for.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Does an exothermic reaction always break fewer bonds than it forms?
cards.back: No; total energies of breaking and forming matter, not simple bond count.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a bond enthalpy calculation not suitable for without extra data?
cards.back: Directly predicting full ΔH for non-gaseous substances without state corrections.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is AQA Required Practical 2 about?
cards.back: Measuring an enthalpy change using calorimetry.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Name one reaction type that could be used for AQA Required Practical 2.
cards.back: Neutralisation.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why might a polystyrene cup and lid be used in calorimetry?
cards.back: To limit heat transfer to the outside and reduce evaporation.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why should a temperature–time correction be considered?
cards.back: Heat exchange can distort the measured maximum/minimum temperature.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What must be explained in a good calorimetry evaluation?
cards.back: Direction of error, its cause, impact on ΔT/ΔH and a realistic improvement.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why might dissolving hydrated vs anhydrous salts help build a Hess cycle?
cards.back: Two measurable solution enthalpies lead to a common final aqueous state.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: A thermometer is ±0.1°C per reading. What is the uncertainty in ΔT?
cards.back: ±0.2°C: add the absolute uncertainties of initial and final readings.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: For ΔT=6.0°C and ±0.1°C per reading, what is % uncertainty?

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How can a slow thermometer affect exothermic calorimetry?
cards.back: It may miss the highest temperature; ΔT is too small and ΔH less negative.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is 2H₂(g)+O₂(g)→2H₂O(l) not a one-mole formation equation?
cards.back: It forms 2 mol H₂O; halve every coefficient for standard molar formation.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is the H–Cl bond enthalpy not averaged across different molecular environments?
cards.back: HCl is diatomic, with only one H–Cl bond environment.
accept: HCl is diatomic, with only one H–Cl bond environment.
diatomic molecule has only one bond environment
HCl has only one H-Cl bond environment

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the formula and charge of sulfate?
cards.back: SO₄²⁻, charge −2.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the formula and charge of hydroxide?
cards.back: OH⁻, charge −1.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the formula and charge of nitrate?
cards.back: NO₃⁻, charge −1.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the formula and charge of carbonate?
cards.back: CO₃²⁻, charge −2.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the formula and charge of ammonium?
cards.back: NH₄⁺, charge +1.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the formula of aluminium nitrate?
cards.back: Al(NO₃)₃.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the formula of ammonium sulfate?
cards.back: (NH₄)₂SO₄.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the formula of magnesium nitrate?
cards.back: Mg(NO₃)₂.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why must ionic formulae have balanced charges?
cards.back: A compound is neutral: total positive and negative charges sum to zero.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: First step for an unfamiliar molecular-shape question?
cards.back: Draw a Lewis structure, identifying the central atom and its bonding and lone pairs.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How are double and triple bonds counted in VSEPR?
cards.back: Each multiple bond is one region of electron density around the central atom.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What decides a molecule's shape rather than electron geometry?
cards.back: Positions of atoms/bonding regions; lone pairs affect angles but are not named as vertices.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why are lone-pair repulsions stronger than bond-pair repulsions?
cards.back: Lone-pair electron density is closer to the central atom and repels bonding pairs more.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What electron-domain shape results from three domains?
cards.back: Trigonal planar, approximately 120° before lone-pair distortion.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Three electron domains: 2 bonds and 1 lone pair. Shape?
cards.back: Bent (V-shaped), with a bond angle slightly below 120°.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Four electron domains: 2 bonds and 2 lone pairs. Shape?
cards.back: Bent, around 104.5° in H₂O.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Four electron domains: 3 bonds and 1 lone pair. Shape?
cards.back: Trigonal pyramidal, about 107° in NH₃.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Four electron domains: 4 bonds and no lone pairs. Shape?
cards.back: Tetrahedral, about 109.5°.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Five electron domains without lone pairs: shape and angles?
cards.back: Trigonal bipyramidal: 90°, 120° and 180°.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why do lone pairs prefer equatorial sites in a trigonal bipyramid?
cards.back: Fewer 90° interactions, so lone-pair repulsion is reduced.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Five domains: 3 bonds, 2 lone pairs. Shape?
cards.back: T-shaped (e.g. ClF₃), with two equatorial lone pairs.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Five domains: 2 bonds, 3 lone pairs. Shape?
cards.back: Linear (e.g. XeF₂); three lone pairs occupy equatorial sites.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Six domains: 5 bonds and 1 lone pair. Shape?
cards.back: Square pyramidal (e.g. BrF₅), approximately 90° angles.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Six domains: 4 bonds and 2 lone pairs. Shape?
cards.back: Square planar (e.g. XeF₄); lone pairs opposite each other.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why are H₂O bond angles smaller than those in NH₃?
cards.back: H₂O has two lone pairs rather than one, so the bonding pairs are pushed closer together.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What must you count first to predict a molecule's shape?
cards.back: Bonding regions and lone pairs around the central atom.
accept: Bonding regions and lone pairs around the central atom.
Bond pairs and lone pairs around the central atom.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How do you identify δ+ and δ− in a polar bond?
cards.back: More electronegative atom is δ−; the other atom is δ+.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Are polar bonds sufficient for a molecular permanent dipole?
cards.back: No; the bond dipoles must not cancel when the 3D shape is considered.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Compare the permanent dipoles of CO₂ and SO₂.
cards.back: CO₂: none, linear dipoles cancel. SO₂: present, bent dipoles do not cancel.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is NH₃ a polar molecule?
cards.back: N–H bonds are polar and trigonal pyramidal shape prevents cancellation.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does CHCl₃ have a permanent dipole but CCl₄ does not?
cards.back: CHCl₃ is asymmetrical; CCl₄ is symmetrical with cancelling C–Cl dipoles.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Can a non-polar molecule contain polar bonds? Example?
cards.back: Yes. In BF₃ the three polar B–F bond dipoles cancel.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What are the two checks for molecular polarity?
cards.back: Check electronegativity differences in bonds, then whether the 3D dipoles cancel.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How do bond polarities differ from intermolecular forces?
cards.back: Bond polarity concerns uneven sharing within a bond; intermolecular forces act between molecules.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What name does your class use for induced dipole–dipole attractions?
cards.back: Van der Waals' forces (induced dipole–dipole attractions).

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What causes van der Waals' forces?
cards.back: Temporary electron fluctuations make dipoles that induce dipoles in neighbouring particles.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Do non-polar molecules experience van der Waals' forces?
cards.back: Yes; induced dipoles form even without a permanent molecular dipole.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why are van der Waals' forces stronger in I₂ than Cl₂?
cards.back: I₂ has more electrons and a more easily polarised cloud, making stronger induced dipoles.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How do stronger van der Waals' forces affect boiling point?
cards.back: More energy is needed to separate molecules, so the boiling point increases.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is water's boiling point anomalously high?
cards.back: O–H polarity allows H bonds between δ+ H and a lone pair on O of another molecule.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does HF hydrogen bond strongly but HCl not normally?
cards.back: In HF, H is bonded to F; in HCl, H is bonded to Cl, not N, O or F.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is overcome when iodine boils: I–I bonds or van der Waals' forces?
cards.back: Intermolecular van der Waals' forces; I–I covalent bonds stay intact.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: In boiling water, which bonds stay intact?
cards.back: The covalent O–H bonds; intermolecular hydrogen bonds are overcome.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What must be overcome when an ionic solid melts?
cards.back: Strong electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions.
accept: Strong electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens to the strength of induced dipole forces down Group 7?
cards.back: They increase down the group.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: When can a molecule with polar bonds still be non-polar?
cards.back: When its bond dipoles cancel because of the molecule's shape.
accept: When its bond dipoles cancel because of the molecule's shape.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is NH₃'s bond angle smaller than CH₄'s?
cards.back: NH₃ has a lone pair; its stronger repulsion reduces the bond angle.
accept: NH₃ has a lone pair; its stronger repulsion reduces the bond angle.
Lone-pair repulsion in ammonia compresses its bond angle.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: When a hydrogen-bonded liquid boils, which bonds are overcome?
cards.back: Intermolecular hydrogen bonds, not covalent O–H or N–H bonds.
accept: Intermolecular hydrogen bonds, not covalent O–H or N–H bonds.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What pressure is used for AQA standard enthalpy changes?
cards.back: 100 kPa.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Must a standard enthalpy change always be at 298 K?
cards.back: No; a stated temperature is required, often 298 K.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: In an enthalpy definition, what does a substance's standard state specify?
cards.back: Its physical state at standard pressure (100 kPa) and the stated temperature.
accept: Its physical state at standard pressure (100 kPa) and the stated temperature.
its physical state at 100 kPa and a stated temperature
physical state at standard pressure and stated temperature

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Name standard states of water, bromine and carbon at 298 K.
cards.back: H₂O(l), Br₂(l), C(s, graphite).

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What must a standard enthalpy of formation equation produce?
cards.back: Exactly 1 mol of compound from its elements in standard states.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What must a standard enthalpy of combustion equation consume?
cards.back: Exactly 1 mol of substance, burned completely in O₂.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the definition of Hess's law?
cards.back: Reaction enthalpy is route-independent if initial/final states are the same.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the molar enthalpy formula if q_solution is in joules?
cards.back: ΔH = −q_solution/(1000 × n) in kJ mol⁻¹.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does n mean in ΔH = −q/n?
cards.back: Moles of the reaction as written, or of the species named in the definition.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is there a minus sign in ΔH = −q_solution/n?
cards.back: Heat gained by solution equals heat lost by reaction (and vice versa).

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: When finding q=mcΔT, do equation coefficients multiply m?
cards.back: No. m is the mass of material undergoing the temperature change.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What must you do to q in joules before obtaining kJ mol⁻¹?
cards.back: Divide q by 1000, then by the appropriate moles.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: If 2 mol of A react per equation, what is n_reaction from 0.10 mol A?
cards.back: 0.10 ÷ 2 = 0.050 mol of reaction as written.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: In H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O, 0.040 mol NaOH is how many reactions?
cards.back: 0.040 ÷ 2 = 0.020 mol of the equation as written.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: For neutralisation enthalpy per mole of water, which n do you use?
cards.back: Moles of H₂O made, not automatically moles of acid or alkali.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What tells you whether to use n of reactant, product or reaction?
cards.back: The stated definition of ΔH and coefficients in the balanced equation.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: For ΔfH° values, which subtraction order gives reaction ΔH?
cards.back: Sum of products − sum of reactants, including coefficients.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: For ΔcH° values, which subtraction order gives reaction ΔH?
cards.back: Sum of reactants − sum of products, including coefficients.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: For 2CO + O₂ → 2CO₂, how many times each ΔfH°?
cards.back: CO₂ ×2, CO ×2, O₂ ×1; ΔfH°(O₂)=0.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: When should you multiply a Hess enthalpy by 2?
cards.back: When the corresponding chemical equation is doubled.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens to ΔH when you reverse a Hess equation?
cards.back: Change the sign of ΔH.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens to ΔH when you halve every equation coefficient?
cards.back: Halve ΔH for that equation.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How do you check Hess arrows if the formula is forgotten?
cards.back: Follow start → finish through the cycle; reverse arrow = reverse sign.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is ΔfH° of O₂(g) zero at 298 K?
cards.back: O₂(g) is oxygen's element in its standard state.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: When are Hess reaction coefficients NOT extra multipliers?
cards.back: If a supplied ΔH already belongs to the full balanced equation shown.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: In bond enthalpy sums, do you multiply by formula subscripts?
cards.back: Count bonds in each molecule, then multiply by the equation coefficient.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: For 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, how many O–H bonds form?
cards.back: 4 O–H bonds: 2 water molecules ×2 bonds each.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: In hydrogenation of ethene, what happens to unchanged C–H bonds?
cards.back: They cancel between reactants and products; count only the net changes.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is AQA Required Practical 2?
cards.back: Measurement of an enthalpy change using calorimetry.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does a polystyrene cup help in solution calorimetry?
cards.back: It reduces heat transfer between the solution and surroundings.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can a lid improve a calorimetry experiment?
cards.back: It reduces heat exchange with surroundings and evaporation.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the key graph correction in exothermic calorimetry?
cards.back: Extrapolate post-reaction cooling to mixing time to estimate peak T.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What effect does heat loss have on calculated exothermic ΔH?
cards.back: Measured ΔT is too small, so ΔH is less negative than the true value.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does thermometer ±0.1°C mean for a temperature difference?
cards.back: Two readings give ±0.2°C absolute uncertainty in ΔT.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why record temperature against time in an RP2 calorimetry experiment?
cards.back: To extrapolate and estimate a corrected temperature change.
accept: To extrapolate and estimate a corrected temperature change.
to estimate the corrected temperature change
to correct for heat exchange with the surroundings by extrapolation
to extrapolate temperature to the mixing time

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which parts of RP2 affect the calorimetry calculation directly?
cards.back: Measured ΔT, solution mass, heat capacity and reaction moles.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Displacement–time: what does a negative gradient mean?
cards.back: Velocity is negative: motion in the negative direction, not necessarily slowing down.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does zero gradient on a displacement–time graph show?
cards.back: Zero velocity: stationary at that instant or throughout a flat segment.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does the signed area below the axis of a velocity–time graph represent?
cards.back: Negative displacement.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why is total distance different from displacement on a v–t graph?
cards.back: Distance sums all absolute areas; displacement uses signed areas.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: A straight sloping v–t line crosses zero. What changes?
cards.back: Direction changes if velocity changes sign; speed falls to zero then rises.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Acceleration–time area gives which quantity?
cards.back: Change in velocity, not displacement or distance.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: For curved s–t graphs, how is instantaneous velocity found?
cards.back: Find the gradient of the tangent at that time.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How do you identify acceleration on a v–t graph?
cards.back: Gradient Δv/Δt; a horizontal line means zero acceleration.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: On a 30° slope, which component of weight pulls downhill?
cards.back: mg sin30°; the perpendicular component is mg cos30°.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: A horizontal push up a slope does what to the reaction?
cards.back: It adds a component into the surface, increasing the normal reaction.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the moment of two equal opposite forces forming a couple?
cards.back: One force × perpendicular separation of their lines of action.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does the gradient of a displacement vs t² graph give in free fall?
cards.back: g/2, for release from rest with negligible drag.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does the SI prefix pico (p) mean?

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does the SI prefix femto (f) mean?

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does the SI prefix tera (T) mean?
cards.back: 10¹².

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the SI base unit for amount of substance?
cards.back: Mole (mol).

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Fill the gap: the base unit of thermodynamic temperature is ____.
cards.back: Kelvin (K).

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How many joules are in one kilowatt-hour?

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the derived SI unit of resistivity?
cards.back: Ohm metre (Ω m).

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is resolution?
cards.back: The smallest change an instrument can distinguish.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is repeatability?
cards.back: Same result using the same method, equipment and operator.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is reproducibility?
cards.back: Consistent results when the method is repeated under changed conditions.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is precision in measurements?
cards.back: How close repeated readings are to one another.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is accuracy in measurements?
cards.back: How close a measured value is to the true value.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: For quantities multiplied, how do percentage uncertainties combine?
cards.back: Add their percentage uncertainties.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: For quantities added, how do absolute uncertainties combine?
cards.back: Add their absolute uncertainties.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: For a measured quantity squared, what happens to its percentage uncertainty?
cards.back: Double it.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What do error bars usually represent?
cards.back: The range of uncertainty around a measured point.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How is uncertainty in a graph gradient estimated?
cards.back: Compare the steepest and shallowest acceptable gradients.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is an order of magnitude?
cards.back: The nearest power of ten to a quantity.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What stays equal for a particle and its antiparticle?
cards.back: Their rest mass.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What changes sign between a charged particle and its antiparticle?
cards.back: Electric charge.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What changes in a nucleus during alpha decay?
cards.back: Nucleon number −4; proton number −2.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What changes in a nucleus during beta-minus decay?
cards.back: Proton number increases by 1; nucleon number stays the same.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the approximate range of the strong nuclear force?
cards.back: A few femtometres, approximately 3 fm.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What happens to the strong nuclear force at extremely small separations?
cards.back: It becomes repulsive.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Which bosons carry the weak interaction at A-level?
cards.back: W⁺ and W⁻ bosons.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What quantity is conserved in strong but not always weak interactions?
cards.back: Strangeness.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Complete: a meson is a quark plus an _____.
cards.back: Antiquark.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Complete: a baryon contains _____ quarks.
cards.back: Three.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is wave amplitude?
cards.back: Maximum displacement from equilibrium.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is wavelength?
cards.back: Shortest distance between two points in phase.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is phase difference?
cards.back: The difference in position within an oscillation cycle.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What phase difference is half a cycle?
cards.back: π radians or 180°.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is a progressive wave?
cards.back: A travelling disturbance that transfers energy without net mass transfer.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is a transverse wave?
cards.back: Oscillations are perpendicular to energy transfer.
accept: Oscillations are perpendicular to energy transfer.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is a longitudinal wave?
cards.back: Oscillations are parallel to energy transfer.
accept: Oscillations are parallel to energy transfer.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is polarisation evidence for?
cards.back: Transverse oscillations.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why can sound in air not be polarised?
cards.back: It is longitudinal.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Fill the gap: a stationary-wave node has ____ amplitude.
cards.back: A point of zero amplitude.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Fill the gap: an antinode has ____ amplitude.
cards.back: A point of maximum amplitude.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How do stationary waves form?
cards.back: Two coherent waves travel in opposite directions and superpose.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How far apart are adjacent stationary-wave nodes?
cards.back: Half a wavelength, λ/2.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: For a string fixed at both ends, what is the first-harmonic wavelength?
cards.back: Twice the vibrating length, λ = 2L.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How does increasing string tension change wave speed?
cards.back: It increases, proportional to √tension.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is mass per unit length of a string?
cards.back: μ = mass/length, measured in kg m⁻¹.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does coherent mean for two wave sources?
cards.back: Same frequency with constant phase difference.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What path difference produces constructive interference?
cards.back: An integer multiple of λ.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What path difference produces destructive interference?
cards.back: An odd multiple of λ/2.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is fringe spacing?
cards.back: Distance between adjacent bright fringes or adjacent dark fringes.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What happens to fringe spacing if the double-slit separation increases?
cards.back: It decreases.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What happens to fringe spacing if the screen distance increases?
cards.back: It increases.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why is the central white-light double-slit fringe white?
cards.back: All wavelengths have zero path difference there.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Which colour spreads most in a white-light diffraction grating?
cards.back: Red; it has the longest wavelength.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What happens to a single-slit central maximum when the slit narrows?
cards.back: It becomes wider.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the highest possible order for a grating?
cards.back: The largest integer n with nλ ≤ d.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is refractive index?
cards.back: n = c/v for light in the medium.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Which wave property stays unchanged across a stationary boundary?
cards.back: Frequency.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What happens to light wavelength on entering a higher-index medium?
cards.back: It decreases.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: When can total internal reflection occur?
cards.back: Light travels from higher to lower refractive index.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the critical-angle equation for air outside a material?
cards.back: sin c = 1/n.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What causes an optical fibre to guide light?
cards.back: Total internal reflection at its boundary.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is a scalar quantity?
cards.back: Magnitude only; no direction.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is a vector quantity?
cards.back: Magnitude and direction.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the principle of moments?
cards.back: In equilibrium, total clockwise moment equals total anticlockwise moment.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the centre of mass?
cards.back: Point at which an object's mass may be treated as concentrated.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does a negative velocity indicate?
cards.back: Motion opposite to the chosen positive direction.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does a negative acceleration mean?
cards.back: Acceleration opposite to the chosen positive direction.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Is deceleration always a negative acceleration?
cards.back: No; it depends on the chosen positive direction.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How do you get total distance from a velocity–time graph?
cards.back: Add the magnitudes of all areas.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What stays constant horizontally in ideal projectile motion?
cards.back: Velocity; horizontal acceleration is zero.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the vertical acceleration during ideal projectile motion?
cards.back: g downward.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is an impulse?
cards.back: Change in momentum, FΔt.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What condition allows use of conservation of momentum?
cards.back: No external resultant force acts on the system.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is an elastic collision?
cards.back: A collision conserving total kinetic energy.
accept: A collision conserving total kinetic energy.
total kinetic energy stays the same

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is efficiency?
cards.back: Useful energy output divided by total energy input.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the work done by a perpendicular force?
cards.back: Zero.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the elastic limit?
cards.back: Beyond it, unloading leaves permanent deformation.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the limit of proportionality?
cards.back: Point beyond which extension is no longer proportional to force.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the ultimate tensile stress?
cards.back: Maximum tensile stress before breaking.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the spring constant?
cards.back: Force divided by extension within the linear region.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does the area under a force–extension graph represent?
cards.back: Work done in stretching the material.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Define electromotive force (emf).
cards.back: Energy supplied by a source per unit charge.
accept: Energy supplied by a source per unit charge.
work done per unit charge by source

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is an ideal ammeter's resistance?
cards.back: Zero.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is an ideal voltmeter's resistance?
cards.back: Infinite.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What condition is required for Ohm's law?
cards.back: Constant physical conditions, including temperature.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why does a filament lamp's I–V curve flatten at high voltage?
cards.back: Its filament heats up and resistance rises.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why is a diode's current very small in reverse bias?
cards.back: It strongly resists current in the reverse direction.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is an NTC thermistor?
cards.back: A component whose resistance falls as temperature rises.
accept: A component whose resistance falls as temperature rises.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is a superconductor?
cards.back: A material with zero resistivity below its critical temperature.
accept: A material with zero resistivity below its critical temperature.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How is current shared at a junction?
cards.back: Total current entering equals total current leaving.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: In a series circuit, which quantity is the same everywhere?
cards.back: Current.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: In a parallel circuit, which quantity is the same across branches?
cards.back: Potential difference.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does the potential-divider output depend on?
cards.back: The proportion of the total resistance across the output.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the intercept of a V–I graph for a cell?
cards.back: The emf.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the magnitude of a cell's V–I gradient?
cards.back: Its internal resistance.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why use a micrometer for a wire's diameter?
cards.back: Small diameter needs a high-resolution measurement.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is angular speed?
cards.back: Angle swept per second, ω = 2πf.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the direction of centripetal acceleration?
cards.back: Towards the centre of the circle.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Does centripetal force do work in uniform circular motion?
cards.back: No; it is perpendicular to instantaneous velocity.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What stays constant in uniform circular motion?
cards.back: Speed, not velocity.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Where is speed greatest in simple harmonic motion?
cards.back: At the equilibrium position.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Where is acceleration greatest in magnitude in SHM?
cards.back: At the extremes of displacement.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: In SHM, what is the phase difference between a and x?
cards.back: π radians (180°).

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How does period depend on mass for a spring oscillator?
cards.back: T ∝ √m.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is natural frequency?
cards.back: Frequency of free oscillations without a driving force.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How does damping affect resonance?
cards.back: Lowers and broadens the peak amplitude.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is internal energy?
cards.back: Sum of random molecular kinetic and potential energies.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What happens to average molecular kinetic energy during melting?
cards.back: It stays approximately constant at fixed temperature.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is absolute zero?
cards.back: The temperature corresponding to 0 K.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why use kelvin for gas equations?
cards.back: Kelvin is an absolute thermodynamic temperature scale.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the pressure of an ideal gas caused by?
cards.back: Molecular collisions with the container walls.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How is rms speed related to mean square speed?
cards.back: rms speed is √(mean square speed).

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the average translational kinetic energy per ideal gas molecule?

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: For an ideal gas at constant volume, how does p depend on T?
cards.back: Pressure is proportional to kelvin temperature.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why is gravitational potential negative?
cards.back: The reference is zero at infinity; attraction lowers potential.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is an equipotential surface?
cards.back: A surface of equal gravitational potential.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How does field strength vary with distance from a point mass?
cards.back: It follows an inverse-square law.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What direction do electric field lines point?
cards.back: Direction of force on a positive test charge.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How does field strength vary with distance from a point charge?
cards.back: It follows an inverse-square law.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What happens to capacitor discharge current over time?
cards.back: Its magnitude decreases exponentially.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How is energy stored in a capacitor expressed?
cards.back: E = ½QV.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What force does a stationary charge feel in a magnetic field?
cards.back: No magnetic force.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: When is magnetic force on a moving charge greatest?
cards.back: When its velocity is perpendicular to the field.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does magnetic flux measure?
cards.back: Field strength times area component normal to the field.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why are transformer cores laminated?
cards.back: To reduce eddy-current energy losses.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: For an ideal transformer, how are input and output power related?
cards.back: They are equal.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is mass defect?
cards.back: Difference between separate nucleon mass and nuclear mass.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does higher binding energy per nucleon generally mean?
cards.back: Greater nuclear stability.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is activity?
cards.back: Number of nuclear decays per second.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Fill the gap: radioactive activity is measured in ____.
cards.back: Becquerel (Bq).

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is half-life?
cards.back: Time for activity or undecayed nuclei to halve.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the relationship between half-life and decay constant?
cards.back: T½ = ln 2/λ.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is induced fission?
cards.back: An absorbed neutron triggers splitting of a heavy nucleus.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: In ultrasound, what produces the returning echoes?
cards.back: Changes in acoustic impedance at tissue boundaries.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is attenuation of an ultrasound wave?
cards.back: Reduction in intensity as the wave travels.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the purpose of an X-ray contrast agent?
cards.back: Increase differences in X-ray attenuation between tissues.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is a CT scan built from?
cards.back: X-ray measurements from multiple directions.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why is a radionuclide tracer useful in imaging?
cards.back: Emitted radiation reveals its distribution in the body.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the relative isotopic mass?
cards.back: Isotope mass relative to 1/12 of a carbon-12 atom.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why are successive ionisation energies always positive?
cards.back: Removing an electron requires energy to overcome attraction.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What causes a large jump between successive ionisation energies?
cards.back: The next electron is removed from an inner shell.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is 4s filled before 3d?
cards.back: 4s is initially lower in energy in neutral atoms.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why are 4s electrons removed before 3d electrons from transition-metal ions?
cards.back: The 4s electrons become higher in energy in these ions.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is meant by an isotope?
cards.back: Atoms of one element with different numbers of neutrons.

cards.subject: Chemistry
