cards.front: What does the molecular-ion peak show in a mass spectrum?
cards.back: The relative molecular mass of the molecular ion.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does concentration in mol dm⁻³ mean?
cards.back: Moles of solute per cubic decimetre of solution.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the limiting reagent?
cards.back: Reactant that runs out first and limits product formed.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is an empirical formula?
cards.back: Simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a molecular formula?
cards.back: Actual number of atoms of each element per molecule.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a standard solution?
cards.back: A solution of accurately known concentration.
accept: A solution of accurately known concentration.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a concordant titre?
cards.back: A titre close to other consistent repeat titres.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a back titration?
cards.back: Finding excess reagent left after a reaction, then finding how much reacted.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does the ideal gas equation assume about intermolecular forces?
cards.back: They are negligible.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does the ideal gas equation assume about particle volume?
cards.back: Molecular volume is negligible compared with container volume.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is covalent bonding?
cards.back: A shared pair of electrons between atoms.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does graphite conduct electricity?
cards.back: Each carbon contributes a delocalised electron.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is diamond so hard?
cards.back: Strong covalent bonds extend throughout a 3D lattice.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does ice float on water?
cards.back: Its hydrogen-bonded open lattice makes it less dense.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What must a molecule have to form hydrogen bonds with another of itself?
cards.back: Hydrogen bonded to N, O or F, with an available lone pair.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a permanent dipole?
cards.back: Unequal electron distribution giving lasting partial charges.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is an exothermic reaction?
cards.back: A reaction that releases heat to the surroundings; ΔH is negative.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is an endothermic reaction?
cards.back: A reaction that absorbs heat from the surroundings; ΔH is positive.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the standard state of a substance?
cards.back: Its most stable physical form under specified standard conditions.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why are bond enthalpies usually positive?
cards.back: Energy is needed to break bonds.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: In q = mcΔT, what mass normally appears?
cards.back: Mass of the substance whose temperature change is measured.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is one frequent source of error in simple calorimetry?
cards.back: Heat exchange with surroundings.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the sign of ΔH for complete combustion?
cards.back: Negative.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is activation energy?
cards.back: Minimum energy required for a successful collision.
accept: Minimum energy required for a successful collision.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is collision frequency?
cards.back: Number of particle collisions per unit time.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How does increasing temperature change the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve?
cards.back: It broadens, lowers its peak and shifts to higher energies.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does heating increase reaction rate disproportionately?
cards.back: A larger fraction of particles exceed activation energy.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a catalyst do to activation energy?
cards.back: It provides an alternative route with lower activation energy.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does increasing concentration usually increase?
cards.back: The frequency of reactant collisions.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does increasing gas pressure usually increase?
cards.back: The frequency of reactant collisions.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does the area under a Maxwell–Boltzmann curve represent?
cards.back: Total number of molecules in the sample.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What defines dynamic equilibrium?
cards.back: Forward and reverse reaction rates are equal in a closed system.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: At equilibrium, are reactant and product concentrations necessarily equal?
cards.back: No; they are constant, not necessarily equal.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How does a catalyst affect the equilibrium position?
cards.back: It does not change it.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which change affects the value of Kc?
cards.back: Temperature.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How does increased pressure shift gaseous equilibrium?
cards.back: Towards the side with fewer gas molecules.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: When does changing pressure have no equilibrium-position effect?
cards.back: When both sides have equal numbers of gas molecules.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What goes into the Kc expression?
cards.back: Equilibrium concentrations, each raised to its coefficient.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which species are omitted from a Kc expression?
cards.back: Pure solids and pure liquids.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How does increasing temperature affect an exothermic equilibrium?
cards.back: Shifts equilibrium towards reactants.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Does changing initial concentration change Kc at fixed temperature?
cards.back: No.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is oxidation in electron terms?
cards.back: Loss of electrons.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is reduction in electron terms?
cards.back: Gain of electrons.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is an oxidising agent?
cards.back: Species that accepts electrons and is reduced.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a reducing agent?
cards.back: Species that donates electrons and is oxidised.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the oxidation state of a free element?
cards.back: Zero.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the oxidation state of oxygen in a peroxide?

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is disproportionation?
cards.back: One element is simultaneously oxidised and reduced.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the total oxidation-state sum in an ion?
cards.back: The ion's overall charge.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How does atomic radius change across Period 3?
cards.back: It generally decreases from Na to Ar.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is the first ionisation energy of Al below Mg?
cards.back: Al loses a higher-energy 3p electron.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is the first ionisation energy of S below P?
cards.back: Paired 3p electrons repel, easing removal.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which Period 3 element has the highest melting point?
cards.back: Silicon.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does silicon have a very high melting point?
cards.back: It has a giant covalent lattice with many strong bonds.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does phosphorus have a lower melting point than silicon?
cards.back: Simple P₄ molecules have weaker intermolecular forces.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does sulfur have a higher melting point than phosphorus?
cards.back: S₈ molecules have more electrons and stronger van der Waals' forces.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does argon melt at a very low temperature?
cards.back: Monatomic particles have weak van der Waals' forces.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which block contains an element whose outermost electron enters a p subshell?
cards.back: p block.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How does first ionisation energy change down Group 2?
cards.back: It decreases.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What forms when a Group 2 metal reacts with water?
cards.back: A metal hydroxide and hydrogen.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the trend in Group 2 hydroxide solubility?
cards.back: Solubility increases down the group.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the trend in Group 2 sulfate solubility?
cards.back: Solubility decreases down the group.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which Group 2 sulfate is essentially insoluble?
cards.back: Barium sulfate, BaSO₄.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which Group 2 hydroxide is an antacid?
cards.back: Magnesium hydroxide.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which Group 2 compound is commonly used to reduce soil acidity?
cards.back: Calcium hydroxide.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which Group 2 oxide can remove sulfur dioxide from flue gases?
cards.back: Calcium oxide.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why acidify the barium-chloride sulfate test?
cards.back: To remove carbonate interference.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What observation indicates sulfate ions in the barium-ion test?
cards.back: A white barium sulfate precipitate.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which Group 2 metal is used to extract titanium from TiCl₄?
cards.back: Magnesium.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How does halogen electronegativity change down Group 7?
cards.back: It decreases.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How do halogen boiling points change down Group 7?
cards.back: They increase.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why do halogen boiling points rise down the group?
cards.back: More electrons produce stronger van der Waals' forces.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which is the stronger oxidising agent: chlorine or bromine?
cards.back: Chlorine.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How does oxidising strength change down Group 7?
cards.back: It decreases.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How does reducing strength of halide ions change down the group?
cards.back: It increases.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Can bromine displace chloride ions from solution?
cards.back: No; bromine is a weaker oxidising agent.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What colour precipitate indicates chloride with silver ions?
cards.back: White (AgCl).

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What colour precipitate indicates bromide with silver ions?
cards.back: Cream (AgBr).

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What colour precipitate indicates iodide with silver ions?
cards.back: Yellow (AgI).

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which silver halide dissolves in dilute ammonia?
cards.back: AgCl.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which silver halide dissolves in concentrated ammonia, but not dilute?
cards.back: AgBr.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which silver halide is insoluble in ammonia?
cards.back: AgI.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why acidify silver nitrate in a halide test?
cards.back: To prevent carbonate or hydroxide interference.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is disproportionation of chlorine in cold alkaline solution?
cards.back: Cl₂ forms chloride and chlorate(I) ions.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why are iodide ions better reducing agents than chloride ions?
cards.back: Iodide loses an electron more easily.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a homologous series?
cards.back: Compounds with the same functional group and general formula.
accept: Compounds with the same functional group and general formula.
same functional group and general formula
same functional group and similar chemical reactions

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a functional group?
cards.back: The part of a molecule responsible for its characteristic reactions.
accept: The part of a molecule responsible for its characteristic reactions.
part of a molecule responsible for its reactions

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a structural isomer?
cards.back: Same molecular formula, different structural formula.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a position isomer?
cards.back: Same skeleton and group type, but in a different position.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is chain isomerism?
cards.back: Same molecular formula but a different carbon skeleton.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does 'displayed formula' show?
cards.back: Every atom and every covalent bond.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a skeletal formula?
cards.back: A line representation omitting C symbols and most attached H atoms.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a curly arrow represent in an organic mechanism?
cards.back: Movement of an electron pair.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the general formula for an acyclic alkane?
cards.back: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What carbon–carbon bonds occur in alkanes?
cards.back: Only single covalent bonds.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a free radical?
cards.back: A species with an unpaired electron.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What begins a free-radical substitution chain?
cards.back: Homolytic bond fission producing radicals.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a propagation step?
cards.back: A radical reacts to form another radical.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a termination step?
cards.back: Two radicals combine and remove radicals from the chain.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why are alkanes relatively unreactive?
cards.back: Strong, mostly non-polar C–C and C–H bonds.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is cracking?
cards.back: Breaking large hydrocarbons into smaller hydrocarbons.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is complete combustion of a hydrocarbon?
cards.back: Reaction with sufficient oxygen producing CO₂ and H₂O.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What bond property makes halogenoalkanes reactive?
cards.back: The C–halogen bond is polar.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is nucleophilic substitution?
cards.back: A nucleophile replaces another atom or group.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does hydrolysis mean?
cards.back: Breaking a bond by reaction with water.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which haloalkane reacts fastest in hydrolysis: fluoro or iodo?
cards.back: Iodoalkane, because its C–I bond is weaker.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens in elimination from a halogenoalkane?
cards.back: H and a halogen leave, creating a C=C bond.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the main type of product from nucleophilic substitution by OH⁻?
cards.back: An alcohol.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the organic product type from substitution by CN⁻?
cards.back: A nitrile.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why are CFCs damaging in the stratosphere?
cards.back: UV releases chlorine radicals that destroy ozone.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the general formula for an acyclic monoalkene?
cards.back: CₙH₂ₙ.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which part of an alkene reacts with an electrophile?
cards.back: Its electron-rich C=C double bond.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is electrophilic addition?
cards.back: An electrophile reacts across a multiple bond.
accept: An electrophile reacts across a multiple bond.
addition of an electrophile across a double bond

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What colour change indicates an alkene with bromine water?
cards.back: Orange to colourless.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What condition permits E/Z isomerism around a C=C bond?
cards.back: Each double-bond carbon has two different groups.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does E mean in E/Z stereoisomerism?
cards.back: Higher-priority groups are on opposite sides.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does Z mean in E/Z stereoisomerism?
cards.back: Higher-priority groups are on the same side.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What forms when ethene undergoes addition polymerisation?
cards.back: Poly(ethene).

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why are addition polymers often chemically unreactive?
cards.back: Strong carbon–carbon backbones lack easily attacked functional groups.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What group identifies an alcohol?
cards.back: Hydroxyl, –OH.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does oxidising a primary alcohol first produce?
cards.back: An aldehyde.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does further oxidation of a primary alcohol produce?
cards.back: A carboxylic acid.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does oxidation of a secondary alcohol produce?
cards.back: A ketone.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why are tertiary alcohols resistant to normal oxidation?
cards.back: No hydrogen on the carbon attached to –OH.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What forms when an alcohol undergoes dehydration?
cards.back: An alkene and water.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens when alcohols react with sodium?
cards.back: An alkoxide and hydrogen form.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why are small alcohols soluble in water?
cards.back: They form hydrogen bonds with water.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a broad O–H infrared absorption suggest?
cards.back: An alcohol or carboxylic acid.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a strong absorption near 1700 cm⁻¹ suggest?
cards.back: A carbonyl C=O group.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a fingerprint region help identify?
cards.back: A specific compound by comparing its IR spectrum.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does the molecular-ion peak indicate?
cards.back: Relative molecular mass.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the purpose of a chemical test for an organic group?
cards.back: To identify a functional group by a characteristic observation.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is standard entropy?
cards.back: Absolute entropy of 1 mol of substance at stated standard conditions.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does positive ΔS mean?
cards.back: The system's entropy increases.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the condition for thermodynamic feasibility using Gibbs free energy?
cards.back: ΔG < 0 at the stated temperature.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Does thermodynamic feasibility guarantee a fast reaction?
cards.back: No; kinetic barriers can make it slow.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a rate equation?
cards.back: An experimentally determined relationship between rate and reactant concentrations.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a zero-order reaction with respect to A?
cards.back: Rate is independent of [A].

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a first-order reaction with respect to A?
cards.back: Rate is proportional to [A].

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a second-order reaction with respect to A?
cards.back: Rate is proportional to [A]².

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does the rate constant k depend on?
cards.back: Temperature, and any catalyst present.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: For a first-order reaction, what is the unit of k?
cards.back: s⁻¹.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the Arrhenius plot gradient for ln k against 1/T?
cards.back: −Ea/R.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Fill the gap: a Brønsted–Lowry acid is a proton ____.
cards.back: A proton donor.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Fill the gap: a Brønsted–Lowry base is a proton ____.
cards.back: A proton acceptor.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a conjugate acid–base pair?
cards.back: Two species differing by one proton.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a strong acid?
cards.back: An acid that fully dissociates in aqueous solution.
accept: An acid that fully dissociates in aqueous solution.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a weak acid?
cards.back: An acid that only partially dissociates in aqueous solution.
accept: An acid that only partially dissociates in aqueous solution.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is Ka?
cards.back: The acid dissociation equilibrium constant.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a larger Ka usually indicate?
cards.back: A stronger weak acid.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Fill the gap: pKa = ____.
cards.back: −log₁₀Ka.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the ionic product of water, Kw?

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: At 25 °C, what is Kw?
cards.back: 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which two components commonly form an acidic buffer?
cards.back: A weak acid and its conjugate base.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the equivalence point in a titration?
cards.back: The point where reactants have reacted in their stoichiometric ratio.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a more positive standard reduction potential mean?
cards.back: Greater tendency to gain electrons under standard conditions.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Does positive Ecell guarantee a fast reaction?
cards.back: No; it indicates feasibility, not rate.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the standard hydrogen electrode assigned?

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is ligand substitution?
cards.back: Replacement of one ligand by another.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is bidentate?
cards.back: A ligand donating two lone pairs to the same metal ion.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the chelate effect?
cards.back: Multidentate ligand substitution often favoured by entropy increase.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a chiral centre?
cards.back: Usually a carbon bonded to four different groups.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a racemic mixture?
cards.back: Equal amounts of two enantiomers.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a racemic mixture do to plane-polarised light?
cards.back: Produces no net rotation.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the functional group in an aldehyde?
cards.back: Terminal carbonyl group, –CHO.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the functional group in a ketone?
cards.back: Carbonyl group between two carbon atoms.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What forms when a ketone is reduced?
cards.back: A secondary alcohol.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What forms when an aldehyde is reduced?
cards.back: A primary alcohol.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which carbonyl compound gives a positive Tollens' test?
cards.back: An aldehyde.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the carboxyl functional group?
cards.back: –COOH.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What causes the acidity of a carboxylic acid?
cards.back: It can donate a proton from –COOH.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is esterification?
cards.back: Formation of an ester from a carboxylic acid and alcohol.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is hydrolysis of an ester?
cards.back: Breaking the ester linkage using water.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does an acyl chloride contain?
cards.back: The –COCl functional group.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is delocalisation in benzene?
cards.back: Electrons are shared across the benzene ring rather than fixed between pairs of atoms.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does benzene favour substitution over addition?
cards.back: Addition would disrupt benzene's stable delocalised electron ring.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is electrophilic substitution?
cards.back: An electrophile replaces an atom or group, commonly H, on a ring.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What makes amines basic?
cards.back: A nitrogen lone pair can accept a proton.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a primary amine?
cards.back: Nitrogen bonded to one carbon-containing group.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What distinguishes condensation polymerisation?
cards.back: Monomers link while eliminating a small molecule.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What bond links monomers in a polyester?
cards.back: Ester linkage, –COO–.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What bond links monomers in a polyamide?
cards.back: Amide linkage, –CONH–.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What groups are found in an alpha-amino acid?
cards.back: –NH₂ and –COOH on the same alpha carbon.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does the number of ¹H NMR signals show?
cards.back: Number of distinct proton environments.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a ¹H NMR integration trace reveal?
cards.back: Relative numbers of protons in each environment.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What causes NMR peak splitting?
cards.back: Coupling with neighbouring non-equivalent protons.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a singlet normally indicate about adjacent equivalent protons?
cards.back: Zero adjacent protons.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does Rf measure in TLC?
cards.back: Distance travelled by spot divided by distance travelled by solvent front.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can chromatography separate mixture components?
cards.back: They distribute differently between stationary and mobile phases.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How does a higher affinity for the stationary phase affect travel?
cards.back: The component travels more slowly.

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: A translation by vector (a, b) does what to (x, y)?
cards.back: Maps it to (x + a, y + b).

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: What does y = f(x − a) do to y = f(x)?
cards.back: Shifts the graph a units right.

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: What does y = f(−x) do to the graph?
cards.back: Reflects it in the y-axis.

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: What does a one-to-one function mean?
cards.back: Distinct inputs have distinct outputs.

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: What is the domain of a function?
cards.back: Its permitted input values.

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: What is the range of a function?
cards.back: Its possible output values.

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: What angle in radians is a full turn?
cards.back: 2π radians.

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: Complete: arc length s = ____ for angle θ in radians.
cards.back: rθ.

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: What is a counterexample?
cards.back: One example showing a universal claim is false.

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: What does the derivative f′(x) represent?
cards.back: The instantaneous gradient of y = f(x).

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: In string-wave RP1, what controls the fundamental frequency?
cards.back: Vibrating length, tension and mass per unit length.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What relation can be tested by plotting f² against tension?
cards.back: A straight line at fixed length and mass per unit length.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Which distance must be measured accurately in a double-slit practical?
cards.back: Slit separation and slit-to-screen distance.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why measure across several interference fringes?
cards.back: It reduces the percentage uncertainty of fringe spacing.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is a key laser safety precaution?
cards.back: Never look directly into the beam.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does the gradient of distance against time squared represent for free fall from rest?

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why is a light gate useful for measuring acceleration?
cards.back: It avoids human reaction-time error in timing.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Which graph gives Young modulus as its gradient?
cards.back: Tensile stress against tensile strain.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why measure a wire's diameter at several positions?
cards.back: To reduce random error and check for variation.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How is wire cross-sectional area obtained from diameter d?
cards.back: A = πd²/4.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does the gradient of resistance against wire length give?
cards.back: ρ/A, for a wire of constant cross-section.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Which graph is used to find a cell's emf and internal resistance?
cards.back: Terminal p.d. V against current I.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why should current not be left flowing unnecessarily in a cell experiment?
cards.back: Heating and changing cell conditions can alter measurements.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What makes a variable 'controlled' in an investigation?
cards.back: It is kept constant to isolate the tested relationship.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why take repeated readings?
cards.back: To identify anomalies and reduce random uncertainty.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does the y-intercept of a graph reveal?
cards.back: The dependent variable when the plotted x-value is zero.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is a zero error?
cards.back: A systematic offset when the true input is zero.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is a fair comparison of two measured gradients?
cards.back: Check whether their uncertainty ranges overlap.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the purpose of a burette?
cards.back: To deliver a measured, variable volume accurately.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the purpose of a volumetric pipette?
cards.back: To transfer a fixed, accurate volume.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why read a burette meniscus at eye level?
cards.back: To avoid parallax error.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does the titre tell you?
cards.back: The volume delivered between initial and final burette readings.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why might calorimetry give a smaller temperature rise than expected?
cards.back: Some energy is transferred to the surroundings.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is extrapolation used in some temperature–time graphs?
cards.back: To estimate temperature change before heat exchange distorts it.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why must the amount in moles match the ΔH definition?
cards.back: Enthalpy change is reported per mole of the specified reaction quantity.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does 1/time approximate in a fixed-endpoint rate practical?
cards.back: Relative initial rate, under comparable conditions.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why must the same visual endpoint be used for rate comparisons?
cards.back: So results represent a consistent extent of reaction.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can a precipitate help identify an ion?
cards.back: Different ions form characteristic insoluble products.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why use a confirmatory test after an initial colour observation?
cards.back: Different substances can give similar initial observations.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What physical property allows distillation to separate liquids?
cards.back: Different boiling points or volatilities.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a thermometer indicate during distillation?
cards.back: The vapour temperature near the collection point.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a positive chemical test establish?
cards.back: Evidence for a functional group, not necessarily a unique compound.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why use more than one analytical observation?
cards.back: Combined evidence reduces ambiguity in identification.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a suitable control variable in a rate experiment?
cards.back: Temperature, if concentration is the independent variable.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does an anomalous reading mean?
cards.back: A result inconsistent with the surrounding trend.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Fill the gap: between MgO and Al₂O₃, the amphoteric oxide is ____.
cards.back: Al₂O₃.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which Period 3 oxide forms phosphoric acid in water?
cards.back: P₄O₁₀.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which Period 3 oxide is a giant covalent solid?
cards.back: SiO₂.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which Period 3 oxide forms a strongly alkaline solution with water?
cards.back: Na₂O.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the oxide formed when magnesium burns in oxygen?
cards.back: MgO.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens when SO₃ reacts with water?
cards.back: It forms sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens when SO₂ dissolves and reacts in water?
cards.back: It produces an acidic solution of sulfurous acid, H₂SO₃.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which Period 3 oxide has an extended covalent network?
cards.back: SiO₂.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does SiO₂ have a high melting point?
cards.back: Many strong covalent bonds must be broken.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why are the oxides of phosphorus and sulfur low melting?
cards.back: They are simple molecular substances with weak intermolecular forces.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is amphoteric behaviour?
cards.back: Reaction with both acids and bases.
accept: Reaction with both acids and bases.
reacts with both acids and bases

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which ions give sodium oxide its ionic lattice?
cards.back: Na⁺ and O²⁻.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does aluminium oxide have a high melting point?
cards.back: Strong electrostatic attractions in its giant lattice.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the formula of phosphorus(V) oxide?
cards.back: P₄O₁₀.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which are the two specified sulfur oxides?
cards.back: SO₂ and SO₃.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Fill the gap: an octahedral complex has coordination number ____.
cards.back: Six.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What coordination number is typical of a tetrahedral complex?
cards.back: Four.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the approximate bond angle of a tetrahedral complex?

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What bond angles occur in an octahedral complex?

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which square-planar platinum complex is used in chemotherapy?
cards.back: Cisplatin.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What coordination number does [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ have?
cards.back: Two.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Fill the gap: [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ is ____ in shape.
cards.back: Linear.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a monodentate ligand?
cards.back: A ligand forming one coordinate bond to a metal centre.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Name one common bidentate ligand.
cards.back: Ethanedioate ion or ethane-1,2-diamine.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a multidentate ligand used in metal complexes?
cards.back: EDTA⁴⁻.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can chelation be entropically favoured?
cards.back: More particles are released when multidentate ligands replace monodentate ones.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What changes a transition-metal complex's observed colour?
cards.back: Ligand, oxidation state or coordination number.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What physical quantity does a colorimeter measure?
cards.back: Absorbance of light.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What law relates absorbance to concentration for dilute solutions?
cards.back: Beer–Lambert law.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens to a catalyst if its active sites are poisoned?
cards.back: Its activity decreases because sites are blocked.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What defines a heterogeneous catalyst?
cards.back: Catalyst and reactants are in different phases.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What defines a homogeneous catalyst?
cards.back: Catalyst and reactants are in the same phase.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Fill the gap: the Haber-process catalyst is ____.
cards.back: Iron.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which catalyst is used in the Contact process?
cards.back: Vanadium(V) oxide, V₂O₅.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is autocatalysis?
cards.back: A reaction product catalyses that reaction.
accept: A reaction product catalyses that reaction.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺ ions act as redox catalysts?
cards.back: They can alternate between oxidation states.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What causes the colour of many transition-metal complexes?
cards.back: Absorption of visible light promoting d-electron transitions.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What colour is aqueous copper(II)?
cards.back: Blue.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What colour is aqueous iron(II)?
cards.back: Pale green.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What colour is aqueous iron(III)?
cards.back: Yellow or pale violet, depending on conditions.
accept: Yellow or pale violet, depending on conditions.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why are 3+ hexaaqua ions more acidic than 2+ ions?
cards.back: Higher charge density polarises O–H bonds more strongly.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What colour is Fe(OH)₂ precipitate?
cards.back: Green.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What colour is Fe(OH)₃ precipitate?
cards.back: Brown.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What colour is Cu(OH)₂ precipitate?
cards.back: Blue.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What colour is Al(OH)₃ precipitate?
cards.back: White.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which metal hydroxide dissolves in excess NaOH to give a colourless solution?
cards.back: Al(OH)₃.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does excess NH₃ do to Cu²⁺ solution after initial precipitation?
cards.back: Dissolves the solid, forming a deep-blue complex.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What complex explains the deep-blue excess-ammonia copper(II) solution?
cards.back: [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens when a metal hexaaqua ion is deprotonated?
cards.back: A hydroxide-containing complex or precipitate can form.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What kind of reaction occurs when NH₃ replaces water ligands?
cards.back: Ligand substitution.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does Al(OH)₃ dissolve in both acid and excess hydroxide?
cards.back: It is amphoteric.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does Kp use instead of concentration?
cards.back: Equilibrium partial pressures.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is partial pressure?
cards.back: Pressure a gas would exert alone in the same volume at the same temperature.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the relationship between partial pressure and mole fraction?
cards.back: pᵢ = xᵢ × total pressure.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Are pure solids included in Kp?
cards.back: No.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Does Kp change when total pressure changes at constant temperature?
cards.back: No.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which change alters Kp for an equilibrium?
cards.back: Temperature.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens to Kp as temperature rises for an exothermic forward reaction?
cards.back: Kp decreases.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens to Kp as temperature rises for an endothermic forward reaction?
cards.back: Kp increases.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: In Kp expressions, what do stoichiometric coefficients become?
cards.back: Powers of partial-pressure terms.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What are standard conditions for standard electrode potential?
cards.back: 298 K, solutions at 1 mol dm⁻³ and gases at 100 kPa.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which electrode is the standard reference?
cards.back: Standard hydrogen electrode.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the role of a salt bridge?
cards.back: Maintains charge balance by allowing ion movement.
accept: Maintains charge balance by allowing ion movement.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Where does oxidation occur in an electrochemical cell?
cards.back: At the anode.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Where does reduction occur in an electrochemical cell?
cards.back: At the cathode.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the emf of a cell from electrode reduction potentials?
cards.back: Ecell = Eright − Eleft, for the cell as written.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does a fuel cell need a continuous fuel supply?
cards.back: Reactants are consumed while generating current.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a rechargeable cell?
cards.back: One whose discharge reactions can be reversed by supplying electrical energy.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a standard electrode potential table show?
cards.back: Standard reduction potentials relative to hydrogen.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What sign of Ecell suggests a reaction is thermodynamically feasible?
cards.back: Positive.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does atom economy measure?
cards.back: Proportion of reactant mass in the desired product.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why are fewer synthesis steps often preferable?
cards.back: They usually reduce waste and cumulative product losses.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can high atom economy benefit a synthesis?
cards.back: It reduces unwanted by-products and resource waste.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does percentage yield measure?
cards.back: Actual product obtained relative to the theoretical amount.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why use a reaction pathway map in synthesis questions?
cards.back: To identify intermediates and compatible functional-group changes.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How are a synthetic intermediate and final product different?
cards.back: The intermediate is converted further; the final product is the target.
accept: The intermediate is converted further; the final product is the target.
intermediate reacts again, final target compound

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the primary structure of a protein?
cards.back: Its amino-acid sequence.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What are two common protein secondary structures?
cards.back: Alpha helices and beta pleated sheets.
accept: Alpha helices and beta pleated sheets.
alpha helix and beta pleated sheet

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a protein's tertiary structure?
cards.back: Its overall three-dimensional folding.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What interactions stabilise protein secondary structure?
cards.back: Hydrogen bonds.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What covalent link can stabilise a protein's tertiary structure?
cards.back: Disulfide bridge, –S–S–.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What group links neighbouring amino acids in a polypeptide?
cards.back: Peptide (amide) link, –CONH–.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a nucleotide made of in DNA?
cards.back: Phosphate, 2-deoxyribose and a base.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which DNA bases pair through hydrogen bonds?
cards.back: A with T; C with G.
accept: A with T; C with G.
adenine with thymine and cytosine with guanine

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the backbone of each DNA strand?
cards.back: Alternating sugar and phosphate units.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How does cisplatin disrupt DNA replication?
cards.back: Platinum forms bonds to DNA bases, hindering strand separation.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is an enzyme's active site?
cards.back: The region that binds a specific substrate.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is an enzyme inhibitor?
cards.back: A substance that reduces the enzyme's catalytic action.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can enzymes be stereospecific?
cards.back: The active-site shape can favour only one enantiomer.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What locates amino-acid spots on some chromatograms?
cards.back: Ninhydrin.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does the mobile phase do in chromatography?
cards.back: It carries the components through the stationary phase.
accept: It carries the components through the stationary phase.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the stationary phase?
cards.back: The phase with which sample components interact while separating.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: In TLC, what is an Rf value?
cards.back: Distance moved by spot divided by distance moved by solvent front.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why compare Rf values under identical conditions?
cards.back: Rf changes with solvent and stationary phase.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a retention time help identify in gas chromatography?
cards.back: A component, when compared under the same conditions.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why may gas chromatography be coupled with mass spectrometry?
cards.back: To separate components and help identify them by mass spectra.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which isotope gives the common hydrogen NMR spectrum?
cards.back: ¹H.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a ¹³C NMR peak correspond to?
cards.back: One distinct carbon environment.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is TMS useful as an NMR reference?
cards.back: It provides the reference at 0 ppm.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does 'chemical shift' describe?
cards.back: Peak position relative to a reference signal, in ppm.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What do two proton NMR signals usually indicate?
cards.back: Two distinct proton environments.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a deuterated solvent reduce in proton NMR?
cards.back: Unwanted solvent ¹H signals.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How does the period of a circular orbit scale with orbital radius?
cards.back: T² is proportional to r³.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is escape speed?
cards.back: Minimum speed to escape a gravitational field without further propulsion.
accept: Minimum speed to escape a gravitational field without further propulsion.
minimum speed to escape gravitational field

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is a geostationary satellite's orbital period?
cards.back: One sidereal day, about 24 hours.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Over which plane must a geostationary satellite orbit?
cards.back: The equatorial plane.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the sign of gravitational potential relative to infinity?
cards.back: Negative at finite distance.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What work is done moving along a gravitational equipotential?
cards.back: Zero.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does the gradient of gravitational potential against r represent?
cards.back: Negative field strength, −gᵣ.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the radius dependence of point-mass gravitational potential?
cards.back: V is proportional to −1/r.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the source of centripetal force for a circular satellite orbit?
cards.back: Gravity.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How does electric force vary with separation between point charges?
cards.back: It follows an inverse-square law.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Can electric charges both attract and repel?
cards.back: Yes.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is ε₀?
cards.back: Permittivity of free space.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the field strength between parallel plates of spacing d?
cards.back: E = V/d.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Where does a positive test charge accelerate in an electric field?
cards.back: Along the field direction.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Where does a negative charge accelerate in an electric field?
cards.back: Opposite to the field direction.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What work is done when charge moves along an equipotential?
cards.back: Zero.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the potential due to point charge Q at distance r?
cards.back: V = Q/(4πε₀r).

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How does electric potential of a point charge vary with distance?
cards.back: It is proportional to 1/r.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How does capacitance change if plate area increases?
cards.back: It increases in proportion to area.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How does capacitance change if plate separation increases?
cards.back: It decreases, inversely with separation.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How does adding a dielectric change capacitance?
cards.back: It increases capacitance.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is relative permittivity?
cards.back: Permittivity of a material divided by permittivity of free space.
accept: Permittivity of a material divided by permittivity of free space.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does area under a V–Q charging graph represent?
cards.back: Energy stored in the capacitor.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: After one discharge time constant, what fraction of charge remains?

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the capacitor's discharge half-life?

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What happens to charging current as a capacitor approaches full charge?
cards.back: It falls towards zero.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What happens to the time constant if resistance doubles?
cards.back: It doubles.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is magnetic flux density's SI unit?
cards.back: Tesla (T).

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the direction of magnetic force relative to velocity?
cards.back: Perpendicular to velocity.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: When is the force on a current-carrying wire zero?
cards.back: When current is parallel to the field.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the cyclotron angular frequency of charge q and mass m?
cards.back: ω = Bq/m in magnitude.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How is magnetic flux through a flat coil defined?
cards.back: Φ = BA cos θ, θ to the coil's normal.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is an electromagnetic force–current balance used to measure?
cards.back: Magnetic flux density.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What determines the magnitude of induced emf?
cards.back: Rate of change of magnetic flux linkage.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How can an induced emf be produced in a stationary coil?
cards.back: Change the magnetic flux through it.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the generator effect?
cards.back: An emf is induced by changing magnetic flux linkage.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How does an ideal transformer relate primary and secondary voltages?
cards.back: Vₛ/Vₚ = Nₛ/Nₚ.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why are transformers used for high-voltage transmission?
cards.back: Higher voltage gives lower current and smaller I²R losses at fixed power.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the role of Lenz's law in induction?
cards.back: Induced effects oppose the flux change causing them.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Which scattering observation supports a tiny, dense nucleus?
cards.back: Rare large-angle alpha-particle deflections.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How does gamma intensity vary with distance from a point source?
cards.back: Approximately 1/r².

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is background count rate?
cards.back: Counts detected without the source contribution.
accept: Counts detected without the source contribution.
counts per second without a source

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Fill the gap: corrected count rate = measured rate − ____.
cards.back: Subtract background count rate.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why is nuclear decay described as random?
cards.back: You cannot predict which particular nucleus will decay next.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does A = λN link?
cards.back: Activity, decay constant and number of undecayed nuclei.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the slope of ln(activity) against time?

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How does nuclear radius scale with nucleon number A?

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does the nuclear radius law imply about density?
cards.back: Nuclear density is approximately constant.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does electron capture do to proton number?
cards.back: It decreases by one.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does beta-plus decay do to proton number?
cards.back: It decreases by one.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What happens to mass number when gamma is emitted?
cards.back: It stays unchanged.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What quantity is conserved in alpha, beta and gamma nuclear equations?
cards.back: Total nucleon number and charge.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does a moderator do in a thermal fission reactor?
cards.back: Slows down neutrons.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What do control rods do in a nuclear reactor?
cards.back: Absorb neutrons to control the reaction rate.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does coolant remove from a reactor core?
cards.back: Thermal energy.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is critical mass in a fission chain reaction?
cards.back: Minimum fissile mass, for a given configuration, sustaining a chain reaction.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why can both fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy nuclei release energy?
cards.back: The products have higher binding energy per nucleon.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What motion does a mass on a spring approximate at small extensions?
cards.back: Simple harmonic motion.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: For a simple pendulum, what is T² proportional to?
cards.back: Pendulum length, for small angles.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How is the period found from ten complete oscillations?
cards.back: Divide total measured time by ten.
accept: Divide total measured time by ten.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why is timing several oscillations better than just one?
cards.back: Reaction-time uncertainty is a smaller fraction.
accept: Reaction-time uncertainty is a smaller fraction.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why must a pendulum's angle be small for the standard formula?
cards.back: The small-angle approximation applies.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is held constant in Boyle's law?
cards.back: Temperature and amount of gas.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What graph tests Boyle's law directly?
cards.back: Pressure against reciprocal volume.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: At fixed temperature, how does pressure vary with volume?
cards.back: Inversely.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is held constant in Charles's law?
cards.back: Pressure and amount of gas.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What graph demonstrates Charles's law using absolute temperature?
cards.back: Volume against temperature in kelvin.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why must temperature be recorded in kelvin for gas-law relationships?
cards.back: Proportionality uses absolute temperature.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the time constant for capacitor discharge through a resistor?
cards.back: RC.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the gradient of ln Q against time during discharge?

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why is a log-linear graph useful in capacitor discharge?
cards.back: Its straight-line gradient gives the time constant.
accept: Its straight-line gradient gives the time constant.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What happens to the capacitor's p.d. during discharge?
cards.back: It decreases exponentially.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How does doubling R affect the discharge time constant?
cards.back: It doubles.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does an oscilloscope time-base setting measure?
cards.back: Time represented by each horizontal division.
accept: Time represented by each horizontal division.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: At 90° to the field, which three factors determine the magnetic force on a wire?
cards.back: Magnetic flux density, current and wire length.
accept: Magnetic flux density, current and wire length.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does the relationship F = BIL assume?
cards.back: The wire is perpendicular to the field.
accept: The wire is perpendicular to the field.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How can a balance reading relate to magnetic force?
cards.back: The change in apparent weight equals the force.
accept: The change in apparent weight equals the force.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How does force vary with current for fixed B and L?
cards.back: Directly proportional.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the gradient of F against I at 90°?
cards.back: BL.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why is it important to keep wire length in the field unchanged?
cards.back: Length affects magnetic force.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does a search coil detect?
cards.back: A changing magnetic flux linkage.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What instrument displays the induced voltage waveform?
cards.back: An oscilloscope.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: When is flux through a flat coil maximum?
cards.back: When the field is perpendicular to its plane.
accept: When the field is perpendicular to its plane.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is magnetic flux for a flat area A and field B?
cards.back: BA cos θ, with θ to the normal.
accept: BA cos θ, with θ to the normal.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why does rotating a coil change its flux linkage?
cards.back: The component of B normal to the coil changes.
accept: The component of B normal to the coil changes.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is flux linkage for N identical turns?
cards.back: NΦ.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What relationship is tested in the gamma inverse-square practical?
cards.back: Intensity is proportional to 1/r².

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What graph gives a straight line for gamma count rate after correction?
cards.back: Corrected count rate against 1/r².
accept: count rate vs reciprocal distance squared

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What should be subtracted from measured count rate?
cards.back: Background count rate.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why is it important to use the source-to-detector distance consistently?
cards.back: It is the separation in the inverse-square relationship.
accept: It is the separation in the inverse-square relationship.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why might gamma count rate vary between repeated measurements?
cards.back: Radioactive decay is random.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What happens to detected intensity when distance doubles ideally?
cards.back: It becomes one quarter.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is an initial-rate method designed to find?
cards.back: Reaction rate close to the start.
accept: Reaction rate close to the start.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is a clock reaction suitable for relative initial rates?
cards.back: The same fixed reaction endpoint is timed.
accept: The same fixed reaction endpoint is timed.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: If the endpoint amount is constant, what is rate proportional to?
cards.back: 1/time.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does the tangent gradient of a concentration–time curve give?
cards.back: Instantaneous reaction rate, with its appropriate sign.
accept: Instantaneous reaction rate, with its appropriate sign.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why are two rate methods useful?
cards.back: They allow comparison of different rate measurements.
accept: They allow comparison of different rate measurements.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why must temperature be controlled when comparing initial rates?
cards.back: Reaction rate and rate constant depend on temperature.
accept: Reaction rate and rate constant depend on temperature.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does EMF measure in an electrochemical cell?
cards.back: Energy transferred per unit charge.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the reference potential of a standard hydrogen electrode?

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the function of a salt bridge?
cards.back: It permits ion movement to maintain charge balance.
accept: It permits ion movement to maintain charge balance.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What can a voltmeter's polarity tell you about a cell?
cards.back: Which electrode is at higher potential.
accept: Which electrode is at higher potential.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is a high-resistance voltmeter useful in EMF measurement?
cards.back: It draws little current.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a titration pH curve plot?
cards.back: pH against volume of titrant added.
accept: pH against volume of titrant added.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the equivalence point on a pH curve?
cards.back: The stoichiometric reaction point.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What determines a suitable titration indicator?
cards.back: Its colour-change range spans the steep pH change.
accept: Its colour-change range spans the steep pH change.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does pH equal at half-neutralisation of a weak acid?
cards.back: pKa.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens to pH near equivalence in many acid–base titrations?
cards.back: It changes rapidly.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is a pH probe preferable to indicator colour for a full curve?
cards.back: It records continuous numerical pH.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a sharp melting point suggest about a solid?
cards.back: It is likely to be relatively pure.
accept: It is likely to be relatively pure.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How does an impurity usually affect a solid's melting point?
cards.back: It lowers and broadens the melting range.
accept: It lowers and broadens the melting range.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the purpose of recrystallisation?
cards.back: To purify a solid product.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why might a separating funnel be useful?
cards.back: It separates immiscible liquid layers.
accept: separates liquids that do not mix

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the purpose of distillation in product purification?
cards.back: To separate liquids by volatility.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why would you calculate percentage yield after purification?
cards.back: To compare recovered product with the theoretical maximum.
accept: To compare recovered product with the theoretical maximum.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What colour is the hydroxide precipitate of aqueous Fe²⁺?
cards.back: Green.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What colour is the hydroxide precipitate of aqueous Fe³⁺?
cards.back: Brown.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What colour is aqueous Cu²⁺?
cards.back: Blue.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does excess ammonia form with aqueous Cu²⁺?
cards.back: A deep-blue copper ammine complex.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can transition-metal complexes change colour on ligand substitution?
cards.back: The energy gap between d orbitals changes.
accept: The energy gap between d orbitals changes.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a precipitate?
cards.back: An insoluble solid formed from a solution.
accept: An insoluble solid formed from a solution.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why should the solvent-front position be recorded?
cards.back: It is needed to calculate Rf.
accept: It is needed to calculate Rf.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a mixture giving several TLC spots suggest?
cards.back: It contains several components.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can TLC help check purity?
cards.back: Multiple spots suggest more than one component.
accept: Multiple spots suggest more than one component.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the stationary phase in TLC typically?
cards.back: A solid adsorbent such as silica.
accept: A solid adsorbent such as silica.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why do TLC components travel different distances?
cards.back: They have different affinities for the phases.
accept: They have different affinities for the phases.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the total energy of a satellite in a circular orbit?
cards.back: E = −GMm/(2r).

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the kinetic energy of a satellite in a circular orbit?
cards.back: Eₖ = GMm/(2r).

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is gravitational potential energy of mass m at distance r from mass M?
cards.back: Eₚ = −GMm/r, taking zero at infinity.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Fill the gap: escape speed from radius r is √(____).
cards.back: 2GM/r.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: As circular orbital radius increases, what happens to a satellite's total energy?
cards.back: It increases towards zero (becomes less negative).
accept: It increases towards zero (becomes less negative)

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: In which direction must a geostationary satellite orbit?
cards.back: In the same direction as Earth's rotation.
accept: In the same direction as Earth's rotation

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does the area under a gravitational field-strength–distance graph give?
cards.back: The magnitude of gravitational potential difference between those positions.
accept: magnitude of gravitational potential difference between those positions

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why is no work done moving a mass along a gravitational equipotential?
cards.back: There is no change in gravitational potential.
accept: There is no change in gravitational potential

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How does a charged particle accelerate in a uniform electric field?
cards.back: With constant acceleration, if other forces are negligible.
accept: With constant acceleration, if other forces are negligible

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does the area under an electric field-strength–distance graph represent?
cards.back: The magnitude of the potential difference across the interval.
accept: magnitude of the potential difference across the interval

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why does a dielectric increase a parallel-plate capacitor's capacitance?
cards.back: Polarisation reduces the field and p.d. for a given stored charge.
accept: Polarisation reduces the field and p.d. for a given stored charge

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How does parallel-plate capacitance depend on plate separation?
cards.back: Inversely proportional: C ∝ 1/d.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What do thumb, first finger and second finger show in Fleming's left-hand rule?
cards.back: Thumb: force; first finger: field; second finger: conventional current.
accept: thumb force first field second current
Thumb: force; first finger: field; second finger: conventional current

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How does the magnetic force direction change if a moving charge is negative?
cards.back: It reverses relative to a positive charge with the same velocity.
accept: It reverses relative to a positive charge with the same velocity

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Fill the gap: induced emf amplitude in a rotating N-turn coil is ____.
cards.back: BANω.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why does a transformer require changing magnetic flux?
cards.back: Changing flux linkage induces an emf in the secondary coil.
accept: Changing flux linkage induces an emf in the secondary coil

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is transformer efficiency in terms of input and output current and p.d.?
cards.back: Efficiency = IₛVₛ/(IₚVₚ).
accept: output power divided by input power

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the RMS current of a sinusoid with peak current I₀?
cards.back: Iᵣₘₛ = I₀/√2.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the RMS voltage of a sinusoid with peak voltage V₀?
cards.back: Vᵣₘₛ = V₀/√2.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the peak-to-peak p.d. of a sinusoidal voltage with peak value V₀?
cards.back: 2V₀.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What two components make a basic buffer?
cards.back: A weak base and its conjugate acid (usually its salt).
accept: weak base and its conjugate acid (usually its salt)

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How does a basic buffer respond to added H⁺?
cards.back: The weak base accepts H⁺, forming its conjugate acid.
accept: weak base reacts with added acid
weak base accepts H⁺, forming its conjugate acid

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How does a basic buffer respond to added OH⁻?
cards.back: Its conjugate acid donates H⁺ to neutralise OH⁻.
accept: Its conjugate acid donates H⁺ to neutralise OH⁻

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why are polyalkenes generally resistant to hydrolysis?
cards.back: Their backbones contain C–C bonds, not hydrolysable ester or amide links.
accept: Their backbones contain C–C bonds, not hydrolysable ester or amide links

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can polyesters be hydrolysed?
cards.back: Their polymer chains contain ester links.
accept: Their polymer chains contain ester links

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can polyamides be hydrolysed?
cards.back: Their polymer chains contain amide links.
accept: Their polymer chains contain amide links

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What links form when a diol reacts with a dicarboxylic acid?
cards.back: Ester links, producing a polyester.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What links form when a diamine reacts with a dicarboxylic acid?
cards.back: Amide links, producing a polyamide.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Give one benefit of recycling polymers rather than discarding them.
cards.back: It can reduce demand for raw materials and landfill waste.
accept: It can reduce demand for raw materials and landfill waste

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is phenylamine generally a weaker base than an aliphatic amine?
cards.back: Its nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring.
accept: Its nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a quaternary ammonium ion?
cards.back: A positively charged nitrogen bonded to four carbon groups.
accept: nitrogen with four organic groups and a positive charge
positively charged nitrogen bonded to four carbon groups

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a use of quaternary ammonium salts?
cards.back: They can act as cationic surfactants.
accept: They can act as cationic surfactants

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a double vertical line (||) mean in cell notation?
cards.back: A salt bridge between half-cells.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a single vertical line (|) show in cell notation?
cards.back: A phase boundary, such as metal against aqueous ions.
accept: phase boundary, such as metal against aqueous ions

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does an electrochemical cell need a salt bridge?
cards.back: To allow ions to move and maintain charge balance.
accept: To allow ions to move and maintain charge balance

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why are 3+ metal aqua ions generally more acidic than comparable 2+ ions?
cards.back: Higher charge density polarises coordinated water O–H bonds more strongly.
accept: Higher charge density polarises coordinated water O–H bonds more strongly

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can carbon monoxide stop haemoglobin transporting oxygen?
cards.back: It binds strongly to Fe²⁺ in haemoglobin, displacing oxygen.
accept: binds to haemoglobin instead of oxygen
It binds strongly to Fe²⁺ in haemoglobin, displacing oxygen

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What bond attaches oxygen to Fe²⁺ in haemoglobin?
cards.back: A coordinate (dative covalent) bond.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How many joules is one electronvolt?

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Which base SI unit is used for amount of substance?
cards.back: Mole (mol).

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What are the base SI units of a newton?
cards.back: kg m s⁻².

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What are the base SI units of a joule?
cards.back: kg m² s⁻².

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is an anomalous reading?
cards.back: A result inconsistent with the trend of the other results.
accept: A result inconsistent with the trend of the other results.
result inconsistent with the trend of the other results

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How does a zero error affect all measurements?
cards.back: It adds a systematic offset.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is a random error's effect on repeated readings?
cards.back: Readings scatter about the mean.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How can repeating readings reduce random uncertainty?
cards.back: Taking a mean reduces its effect.
accept: Taking a mean reduces its effect.
Taking a mean reduces its effect

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why is a graph through the origin not always justified?
cards.back: A systematic offset or real intercept may exist.
accept: A systematic offset or real intercept may exist.
systematic offset or real intercept may exist

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What should an uncertainty normally be rounded to?
cards.back: Usually one significant figure.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the approximate percentage uncertainty in a value x?
cards.back: (Absolute uncertainty / x) × 100%.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How are percentage uncertainties combined for a product of measured quantities?
cards.back: Add the individual percentage uncertainties.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the charge of an up quark?
cards.back: +2/3 of the elementary charge.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the charge of a down quark?
cards.back: −1/3 of the elementary charge.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Which quarks form a proton?
cards.back: uud.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Which quarks form a neutron?
cards.back: udd.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the baryon number of a meson?
cards.back: Zero.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the baryon number of an antibaryon?

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Which conservation law is obeyed in all particle interactions?
cards.back: Conservation of charge.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What carries the electromagnetic interaction?
cards.back: Virtual photons.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Which weak-interaction exchange bosons must you know for AQA AS Physics?
cards.back: W⁺ and W⁻ bosons.
accept: W plus and W minus bosons

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the lepton number of an antilepton?
cards.back: −1 (for its lepton family).

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the role of a neutrino in beta-minus decay?
cards.back: An electron antineutrino balances lepton number.
accept: An electron antineutrino balances lepton number.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the stopping potential of photoelectrons?
cards.back: The reverse p.d. that just stops the fastest photoelectrons.
accept: The reverse p.d. that just stops the fastest photoelectrons.
reverse voltage that stops the fastest photoelectrons
voltage needed to stop the most energetic photoelectrons
reverse p.d. that just stops the fastest photoelectrons

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why does increasing light intensity not raise photoelectron maximum energy?
cards.back: Photon energy depends on frequency, not intensity.
accept: Photon energy depends on frequency, not intensity.
Photon energy depends on frequency, not intensity

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How does increasing light intensity above threshold affect photoelectric current?
cards.back: It can increase current by ejecting more electrons per second.
accept: It can increase current by ejecting more electrons per second.
It can increase current by ejecting more electrons per second

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does the frequency-axis intercept of an Eₖ,max–frequency graph show?
cards.back: The threshold frequency.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does the Eₖ,max–frequency graph gradient equal?
cards.back: Planck's constant h.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What phase difference corresponds to a quarter of a cycle?
cards.back: π/2 radians (90°).

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What happens to wave speed when frequency doubles in the same medium?
cards.back: It stays the same.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Which wave property is fixed by its source across a boundary?
cards.back: Frequency.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why can polarising filters reduce glare?
cards.back: They preferentially transmit one polarisation direction.
accept: They preferentially transmit one polarisation direction.
They preferentially transmit one polarisation direction

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What must be true of the waves at a stationary-wave node?
cards.back: They interfere destructively at all times.
accept: They interfere destructively at all times.
They interfere destructively at all times

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the distance between adjacent stationary-wave nodes?
cards.back: Half a wavelength.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why does a stationary wave not transfer net energy along the medium?
cards.back: Opposite travelling waves carry equal energy in opposite directions.
accept: Opposite travelling waves carry equal energy in opposite directions.
Opposite travelling waves carry equal energy in opposite directions

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the phase relation of particles between adjacent nodes?
cards.back: They oscillate in phase.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the phase relation of particles on either side of a node?
cards.back: They oscillate in antiphase.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the path difference for a first-order bright fringe?
cards.back: One wavelength.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What path difference gives destructive interference?
cards.back: (n + ½) wavelengths, for integer n.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How does fringe spacing change if double-slit separation increases?
cards.back: It decreases.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How does fringe spacing change if screen distance increases?
cards.back: It increases.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why is monochromatic light useful in a double-slit experiment?
cards.back: It gives a single consistent fringe spacing.
