accept: It gives a single consistent fringe spacing.
It gives a single consistent fringe spacing

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why do two independent lamps not produce stable fringes?
cards.back: Their relative phase changes randomly.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does a diffraction grating allow you to measure?
cards.back: Wavelength from the angular positions of maxima.
accept: Wavelength from the angular positions of maxima.
Wavelength from the angular positions of maxima

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the condition for a grating maximum?
cards.back: d sin θ = nλ.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does the critical angle mean?
cards.back: Incidence angle in denser medium for a refracted ray at 90°.
accept: Incidence angle in denser medium for a refracted ray at 90°.
Incidence angle in denser medium for a refracted ray at 90°

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the relationship between refractive index and critical angle?
cards.back: sin c = 1/n, for a boundary with air.
accept: sin c = 1/n, for a boundary with air.
sin c = 1/n, for a boundary with air

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What condition gives equilibrium for three coplanar forces?
cards.back: Their vector sum is zero.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does the gradient of a displacement–time graph give?
cards.back: Velocity, including its sign.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does the area below a negative velocity–time graph represent?
cards.back: Negative displacement.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How is impulse related to momentum?
cards.back: Impulse equals change in momentum.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the SI unit of impulse?
cards.back: N s, equivalent to kg m s⁻¹.
accept: N s, equivalent to kg m s⁻¹.
N s, equivalent to kg m s⁻¹

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does the principle of conservation of momentum require?
cards.back: No resultant external force on the system.
accept: No resultant external force on the system.
No resultant external force on the system

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: When is the net moment of forces zero?
cards.back: In rotational equilibrium.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is a couple's resultant force?
cards.back: Zero.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What quantity does a couple produce even when resultant force is zero?
cards.back: A turning moment.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How does the normal reaction change on an incline without other perpendicular forces?
cards.back: R = mg cos θ.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the weight component down a slope of angle θ?
cards.back: mg sin θ.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does the gradient of an elastic force–extension graph give?
cards.back: The spring constant k.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why does strain have no unit?
cards.back: It is a ratio of two lengths.
accept: It is a ratio of two lengths.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the gradient of a linear stress–strain graph?
cards.back: Young modulus.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How does a brittle material usually fail?
cards.back: With little or no plastic deformation.
accept: With little or no plastic deformation.
With little or no plastic deformation

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does plastic deformation mean?
cards.back: Permanent change of shape after load removal.
accept: Permanent change of shape after load removal.
Permanent change of shape after load removal

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why is an ammeter connected in series?
cards.back: It measures current through the component.
accept: It measures current through the component.
It measures current through the component

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why is a voltmeter connected in parallel?
cards.back: It measures potential difference across the component.
accept: It measures potential difference across the component.
It measures potential difference across the component

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How does a filament lamp's resistance change as it heats?
cards.back: It increases.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why does a diode have a strongly asymmetric I–V graph?
cards.back: It mainly conducts in one direction.
accept: It mainly conducts in one direction.
It mainly conducts in one direction

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the internal resistance of an ideal voltmeter?
cards.back: Infinite.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the internal resistance of an ideal ammeter?
cards.back: Zero.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the terminal p.d. of a discharging cell?
cards.back: ε − Ir.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does the y-intercept of terminal p.d. against current show?
cards.back: The cell's emf.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does the negative gradient of terminal p.d. against current show?
cards.back: Internal resistance.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What happens to an NTC thermistor's resistance as temperature rises?
cards.back: It decreases.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What happens to an LDR's resistance in brighter light?
cards.back: It decreases.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How does total resistance change when another resistor is added in parallel?
cards.back: It decreases.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the p.d. across components connected in parallel?
cards.back: The same across each branch.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What happens to current at a circuit junction?
cards.back: Total current entering equals total current leaving.
accept: Total current entering equals total current leaving.
Total current entering equals total current leaving

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: When does an SHM oscillator have maximum speed?
cards.back: At its equilibrium position.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How does the pendulum period vary with length for small angles?
cards.back: T ∝ √L.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How does spring–mass oscillation period vary with mass?
cards.back: T ∝ √m.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does resonance occur when the driving frequency approaches?
cards.back: The natural frequency of the oscillator.
accept: The natural frequency of the oscillator.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why does damping reduce resonant amplitude?
cards.back: Energy is dissipated each cycle.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does a velocity–time graph's gradient give in SHM?
cards.back: Instantaneous acceleration.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the difference between specific and latent heat?
cards.back: Specific heat changes temperature; latent heat changes state.
accept: Specific heat changes temperature; latent heat changes state.
Specific heat changes temperature; latent heat changes state

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why does temperature stay steady during an ideal phase change?
cards.back: Energy changes intermolecular potential energy.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the internal energy of an ideal monatomic gas?
cards.back: Total random translational kinetic energy of its atoms.
accept: Total random translational kinetic energy of its atoms.
Total random translational kinetic energy of its atoms

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How is a kelvin temperature related to Celsius temperature?

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does pV/T equal for a fixed amount of ideal gas?
cards.back: A constant.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why must T be in kelvin for gas-law equations?
cards.back: Gas pressure/volume proportions use absolute temperature.
accept: Gas pressure/volume proportions use absolute temperature.
Gas pressure/volume proportions use absolute temperature

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What physical process produces gas pressure?
cards.back: Particle collisions with container walls.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does mean square molecular speed mean?
cards.back: Average of the squared speeds.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does root mean square speed mean?
cards.back: Square root of the mean of squared speeds.
accept: Square root of the mean of squared speeds.
square root of mean squared speed
Square root of the mean of squared speeds

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why does gas internal energy depend only on temperature in an ideal model?
cards.back: Intermolecular potential energy is neglected.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why can a gravitational field not repel a test mass?
cards.back: Gravitational force between masses is always attractive.
accept: Gravitational force between masses is always attractive.
Gravitational force between masses is always attractive

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How do electric and gravitational inverse-square fields differ?
cards.back: Electric forces can attract or repel; gravity attracts only.
accept: Electric forces can attract or repel; gravity attracts only.
Electric forces can attract or repel; gravity attracts only

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does the gradient of gravitational potential against radial distance give?
cards.back: Negative radial field strength.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the orbital speed in a circular orbit of radius r about mass M?

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the time period for a circular orbit of radius r around mass M?
cards.back: 2π√(r³/GM).

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the unit of electric field strength?
cards.back: N C⁻¹, equivalent to V m⁻¹.
accept: N C⁻¹, equivalent to V m⁻¹.
N C⁻¹, equivalent to V m⁻¹

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How does electric force on a charged object relate to field strength?

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does unloading to zero force with non-zero extension show?
cards.back: Plastic deformation.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the energy stored when a Hookean spring extends by x?
cards.back: ½kx².

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does the area under a stress–strain curve per unit volume represent?
cards.back: Work done per unit volume.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What happens to stiffness if a wire of the same material is made longer?
cards.back: It decreases for unchanged cross-section.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Can longitudinal waves be plane-polarised?
cards.back: No.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Which way do particles oscillate in a transverse wave?
cards.back: Perpendicular to propagation.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Which way do particles oscillate in a longitudinal wave?
cards.back: Parallel to propagation.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Does frequency change when a wave enters a different medium?
cards.back: No.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What happens to wavelength if wave speed halves at fixed frequency?
cards.back: It halves.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How far apart are adjacent nodes and antinodes in a stationary wave?
cards.back: One quarter of a wavelength.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What determines the fundamental wavelength of a string fixed at both ends?
cards.back: Twice the string length.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What happens to string wave speed if tension becomes four times as large?
cards.back: It doubles at fixed mass per unit length.
accept: It doubles at fixed mass per unit length.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What happens to ray direction when light enters a more optically dense medium obliquely?
cards.back: It bends towards the normal.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What happens to light speed when refractive index increases?
cards.back: It decreases.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: For total internal reflection, which medium must the ray begin in?
cards.back: The optically denser medium.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What two observations show total internal reflection?
cards.back: No refracted ray; light reflects into original medium.
accept: No refracted ray; light reflects into original medium.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the rate of flow of charge?
cards.back: Electric current.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why does a metal's resistance often rise with temperature?
cards.back: Greater lattice vibrations increase electron scattering.
accept: Greater lattice vibrations increase electron scattering.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does resistivity measure?
cards.back: Resistance normalised for a material's length and cross-section.
accept: Resistance normalised for a material's length and cross-section.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What happens to resistance if a wire's length doubles at constant area?
cards.back: It doubles.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What happens to resistance if a wire's area doubles at constant length?
cards.back: It halves.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does the gradient of an I–V graph give for an ohmic resistor?
cards.back: Conductance, 1/R.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does the gradient of a V–I graph give for an ohmic resistor?
cards.back: Resistance.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: For series resistors, what happens to the total potential difference?
cards.back: It equals the sum of individual p.d.s.
accept: It equals the sum of individual p.d.s.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the direction of conventional current outside a cell?
cards.back: From positive to negative terminal.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the purpose of a potential divider?
cards.back: Produce a fraction of the supply p.d.
accept: Produce a fraction of the supply p.d.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: In a stationary-wave string practical, what is measured between adjacent nodes?
cards.back: Half a wavelength.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why is tension a controlled variable in a string-frequency investigation?
cards.back: Tension changes wave speed.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What quantity must be known to calculate wave speed using v = √(T/μ)?
cards.back: Mass per unit length, μ.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: In Young's double-slit work, what is the main advantage of measuring several fringe spacings?
cards.back: Reduces percentage uncertainty.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: In double-slit work, what should the screen distance be measured from?
cards.back: From the slits.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why use electronic timing for free-fall measurements?
cards.back: Reduces human reaction-time uncertainty.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: If s is plotted against t² for motion from rest, what does the gradient equal?

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why measure wire diameter at several positions?
cards.back: To check variation and reduce random uncertainty.
accept: To check variation and reduce random uncertainty.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why can a longer wire give a more accurate extension measurement for Young modulus?
cards.back: It produces a larger extension for the same stress, lowering percentage uncertainty.
accept: It produces a larger extension for the same stress, lowering percentage uncertainty.
Improves strain resolution and percentage uncertainty.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: In a resistivity experiment, what two dimensions must be measured?
cards.back: Wire length and cross-sectional area.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: For a wire, how does resistivity relate to R, A and L?
cards.back: ρ = RA/L.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How can emf be found from a V–I graph for a cell?
cards.back: The vertical intercept.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How can internal resistance be found from the terminal p.d.–current graph?
cards.back: Negative of its gradient.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a standard state?
cards.back: Most stable physical state of a substance at stated standard conditions.
accept: Most stable physical state of a substance at stated standard conditions.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is ΔfH° for an element in its standard state zero?
cards.back: It is the reference state for enthalpy of formation.
accept: It is the reference state for enthalpy of formation.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: In combustion enthalpy, how much of the substance must burn?
cards.back: Exactly one mole.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: For formation enthalpy, how much compound is made?
cards.back: Exactly one mole from elements in standard states.
accept: Exactly one mole from elements in standard states.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can experimental combustion enthalpy appear less exothermic than data values?
cards.back: Heat losses or incomplete combustion.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: When using mean bond enthalpies, what state must reacting species have?
cards.back: Gas phase.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the meaning of an enthalpy level below the reactants on a cycle?
cards.back: Lower enthalpy than the reactants.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What stays constant in a closed system at dynamic equilibrium?
cards.back: Concentrations of reactants and products.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Does changing initial concentration alter Kc at fixed temperature?
cards.back: No.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: If forward reaction is endothermic, how does warming affect Kc?
cards.back: It increases.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: If forward reaction is exothermic, how does warming affect Kc?
cards.back: It decreases.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens to Kc when total pressure changes at fixed temperature?
cards.back: No change.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the effect of adding a catalyst on equilibrium time?
cards.back: Equilibrium may be reached sooner.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does sodium have a higher electrical conductivity than sulfur?
cards.back: Sodium is metallic with mobile electrons.
accept: Sodium is metallic with mobile electrons.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What bonding gives aluminium a high melting point compared with sodium?
cards.back: Stronger metallic bonding from higher charge density.
accept: Stronger metallic bonding from higher charge density.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does magnesium usually melt above sodium?
cards.back: Its metallic bonding is stronger.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which Period 3 element forms a giant covalent lattice?
cards.back: Silicon.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens to first ionisation energy down Group 2?
cards.back: It generally decreases.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does shielding increase down Group 2?
cards.back: More occupied electron shells.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is barium sulfate unsuitable for making soluble barium solutions?
cards.back: It is extremely insoluble.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which solid forms when magnesium burns in oxygen?
cards.back: Magnesium oxide, MgO.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the oxidation number of Group 2 metals in their common compounds?

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which metal reacts more readily with water: Ca or Mg?
cards.back: Calcium.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does a white sulfate precipitate form on adding barium ions to sulfate solution?
cards.back: BaSO₄ is insoluble.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What colour is chlorine gas?
cards.back: Pale green.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What colour is bromine at room temperature?
cards.back: Red-brown liquid.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What colour is solid iodine?
cards.back: Grey-black.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which silver halide needs concentrated aqueous ammonia to dissolve?
cards.back: Silver bromide.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which silver halide stays insoluble in concentrated aqueous ammonia?
cards.back: Silver iodide.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a chlorine displacement reaction produce from bromide?
cards.back: Bromine.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens to chlorine in water?
cards.back: Some forms HCl and HClO by disproportionation.
accept: Some forms HCl and HClO by disproportionation.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the disinfecting species formed from dissolved chlorine?
cards.back: Chloric(I) acid, HClO.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is standard enthalpy of atomisation?
cards.back: Enthalpy to form one mole of gaseous atoms from an element in its standard state.
accept: Enthalpy to form one mole of gaseous atoms from an element in its standard state.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is first ionisation enthalpy?
cards.back: Energy to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms.
accept: Energy to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms.
remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is second ionisation enthalpy?
cards.back: Energy to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous 1+ ions.
accept: Energy to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous 1+ ions.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is second electron affinity?
cards.back: Enthalpy for adding one mole of electrons to one mole of gaseous 1− ions.
accept: Enthalpy for adding one mole of electrons to one mole of gaseous 1− ions.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does forming O²⁻ require two electron-affinity steps?
cards.back: Two electrons must be added to O atoms.
accept: Two electrons must be added to O atoms.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: In a Born–Haber cycle, how do you handle forming a 2+ cation?
cards.back: Include both first and second ionisation enthalpies.
accept: Include both first and second ionisation enthalpies.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: For MgCl₂ formation, how many chlorine atomisation terms arise from Cl₂?
cards.back: Two moles of gaseous chlorine atoms.
accept: Two moles of gaseous chlorine atoms.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a negative enthalpy of hydration signify?
cards.back: Energy released when gaseous ions become aqueous ions.
accept: Energy released when gaseous ions become aqueous ions.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why do small highly charged ions usually have more exothermic hydration enthalpies?
cards.back: Stronger attraction to water dipoles.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the entropy change formula from standard molar entropies?
cards.back: ΣS°(products) − ΣS°(reactants).

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: When ΔG = ΔH − TΔS changes sign as temperature varies, what does ΔG = 0 locate?
cards.back: The threshold temperature between predicted feasible and non-feasible conditions.
accept: The threshold temperature between predicted feasible and non-feasible conditions.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why must entropy units be converted before ΔG calculation using kJ?
cards.back: ΔS is usually in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; ΔH in kJ mol⁻¹.
accept: ΔS is usually in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; ΔH in kJ mol⁻¹.
convert entropy from joules to kilojoules

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the rate constant k for a zero-order reaction's rate law rate = k?
cards.back: The constant rate itself.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why do units of k change with overall reaction order?
cards.back: Its units must give rate units when multiplied by concentrations.
accept: Its units must give rate units when multiplied by concentrations.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What are k units for overall first order, with rate in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹?
cards.back: s⁻¹.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What are k units for overall second order?
cards.back: dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What are k units for overall zero order?
cards.back: mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is a slow step important in a proposed reaction mechanism?
cards.back: It can control the overall rate.
accept: It can control the overall rate.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is an initial rate?
cards.back: Rate at the start of reaction, before concentrations change appreciably.
accept: Rate at the start of reaction, before concentrations change appreciably.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a horizontal rate–concentration plot imply for that reactant?
cards.back: Zero order.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How does ln k vary with reciprocal temperature on an Arrhenius plot?
cards.back: It is linear with negative gradient.
accept: It is linear with negative gradient.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How is pH linked to acid concentration if it is a strong monoprotic acid?
cards.back: pH = −log₁₀ c, when fully dissociated.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is a weak acid's [H⁺] less than its initial concentration?
cards.back: It only partially dissociates.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the unit of Ka when defined using concentrations?
cards.back: mol dm⁻³.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is pKa when Ka = 1 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³?

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens to pH when [H⁺] rises tenfold?
cards.back: It decreases by one.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: At 298 K, what is pH + pOH?

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does a weak-acid buffer resist added acid?
cards.back: Its conjugate base accepts added H⁺.
accept: Its conjugate base accepts added H⁺.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does a weak-acid buffer resist added alkali?
cards.back: The weak acid reacts with added OH⁻.
accept: The weak acid reacts with added OH⁻.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What proportion of acid and conjugate base is present when pH = pKa?
cards.back: Equal concentrations.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is an indicator chosen by its transition range?
cards.back: It must change colour within the steep pH region.
accept: It must change colour within the steep pH region.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does pH at the equivalence point depend on?
cards.back: Relative strengths of the acid and base.
accept: Relative strengths of the acid and base.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Can a pH 7 indicator be unsuitable for weak acid–strong base titration?
cards.back: Yes; equivalence pH is above 7.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a displayed formula show that a structural formula may omit?
cards.back: Every bond between atoms.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: In a curly-arrow mechanism, where must the arrow tail start?
cards.back: At a lone pair or a covalent bond.
accept: At a lone pair or a covalent bond.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What distinguishes heterolytic from homolytic fission?
cards.back: Heterolytic gives both electrons to one fragment; homolytic splits them.
accept: Heterolytic gives both electrons to one fragment; homolytic splits them.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a carbocation?
cards.back: A positively charged carbon-containing ion.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What observation shows a positive Tollens' test?
cards.back: Silver mirror or grey silver deposit.
accept: Silver mirror or grey silver deposit.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What observation shows a positive Fehling's test?
cards.back: Brick-red precipitate.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What colour is the 2,4-DNPH precipitate for carbonyl compounds?
cards.back: Orange.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does nucleophilic addition to propanone first create?
cards.back: An alkoxide intermediate.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the functional group of an acyl chloride?
cards.back: –COCl.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What type of reaction commonly involves an acyl chloride?
cards.back: Nucleophilic addition–elimination.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the structural group of an amide?
cards.back: –CONH₂ or substituted –CONHR/–CONR₂.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why do carboxylic acids often boil above similar-sized esters?
cards.back: They can form intermolecular hydrogen-bonded dimers.
accept: They can form intermolecular hydrogen-bonded dimers.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does heating an ester with aqueous acid allow?
cards.back: Reversible acid hydrolysis.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What calculation gives average gas-production rate?
cards.back: Change in gas volume ÷ change in time.
accept: Change in gas volume ÷ change in time.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What units can a gas-volume reaction rate have?
cards.back: cm³ s⁻¹.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How do you find instantaneous rate on a curved graph?
cards.back: Draw a tangent and calculate its gradient.
accept: Draw a tangent and calculate its gradient.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is the gradient negative for disappearing reactant?
cards.back: Its concentration falls with time; rate of disappearance uses −gradient.
accept: Its concentration falls with time; rate of disappearance uses −gradient.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a flat gas-volume–time graph mean?
cards.back: No further gas is produced; gradient and measured rate are zero.
accept: No further gas is produced; gradient and measured rate are zero.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does a gas-producing reaction normally slow over time?
cards.back: Reactant concentrations fall, reducing successful collision frequency.
accept: Reactant concentrations fall, reducing successful collision frequency.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Does heating lower activation energy?
cards.back: No. It increases the fraction of collisions with energy ≥ Eₐ.
accept: No. It increases the fraction of collisions with energy ≥ Eₐ.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens to the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve when a catalyst is added?
cards.back: Nothing at constant temperature; the Eₐ threshold moves left.
accept: Nothing at constant temperature; the Eₐ threshold moves left.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How does greater solid surface area increase reaction rate?
cards.back: More surface particles are accessible to reacting particles.
accept: More surface particles are accessible to reacting particles.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What makes the mixture cloudy in a thiosulfate rate practical?
cards.back: Formation of solid sulfur.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why use 1/t in a fixed-endpoint rate investigation?
cards.back: The same visible change occurs in less time when the reaction is faster.
accept: The same visible change occurs in less time when the reaction is faster.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What are the units of a 1/t relative-rate measure?
cards.back: s⁻¹, if t is measured in seconds.
accept: s⁻¹, if t is measured in seconds.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Give two controls in a temperature–rate practical.
cards.back: Reactant concentrations and total reaction-mixture volume.
accept: Reactant concentrations and total reaction-mixture volume.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is the disappearing-cross endpoint imprecise?
cards.back: Different observers may judge the obscuring time differently.
accept: Different observers may judge the obscuring time differently.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why must an equilibrium system be closed?
cards.back: To prevent loss or gain of substances while reversible reactions continue.
accept: To prevent loss or gain of substances while reversible reactions continue.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: At equilibrium, do reactions stop?
cards.back: No; both directions continue at equal, non-zero rates.
accept: No; both directions continue at equal, non-zero rates.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens if a product is removed at equilibrium?
cards.back: The equilibrium shifts towards the products to replace some of it.
accept: The equilibrium shifts towards the products to replace some of it.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which states count when predicting a pressure shift?
cards.back: Count gaseous moles only; omit solids and liquids.
accept: Count gaseous moles only; omit solids and liquids.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Does adding an inert gas at constant volume shift a gas equilibrium?
cards.back: No; partial pressures of reacting gases remain unchanged.
accept: No; partial pressures of reacting gases remain unchanged.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How many gaseous moles are on each side of N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃?
cards.back: Four on the left; two on the right.
accept: Four on the left; two on the right.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why not use an extremely low temperature in the Haber process?
cards.back: Equilibrium yield rises, but ammonia production becomes too slow.
accept: Equilibrium yield rises, but ammonia production becomes too slow.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why not use an extremely high Haber-process pressure?
cards.back: Compression is costly and demands expensive high-pressure equipment.
accept: Compression is costly and demands expensive high-pressure equipment.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why use an iron catalyst in ammonia production?
cards.back: Faster approach to equilibrium; it does not change equilibrium yield.
accept: Faster approach to equilibrium; it does not change equilibrium yield.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: In an equilibrium mole table, how much H₂ is used to make 0.60 mol HI?
cards.back: 0.30 mol, for H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How do you convert equilibrium moles to concentration?
cards.back: Concentration = moles ÷ volume in dm³.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: For A + B ⇌ 2C, how is [C] found once [C]² is known?
cards.back: Take the positive square root.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Does a large Kc mean the reaction is fast?
cards.back: No; it means products are favoured at equilibrium, not a fast rate.
accept: No; it means products are favoured at equilibrium, not a fast rate.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: On a concentration–time graph, what causes an immediate vertical jump?
cards.back: Direct addition or removal of a species, before gradual re-equilibration.
accept: Direct addition or removal of a species, before gradual re-equilibration.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What oxidation state does fluorine always have in its compounds?

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is hydrogen's oxidation state in NaH?
cards.back: −1, because it is a metal hydride.
accept: −1, because it is a metal hydride.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is oxygen's oxidation state in OF₂?
cards.back: +2; each fluorine is −1.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is sulfur's oxidation state in SO₄²⁻?

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is nitrogen's oxidation state in NH₄⁺?

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is nitrogen's oxidation state in NO₃⁻?

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is manganese's oxidation state in MnO₄⁻?

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is chromium's oxidation state in Cr₂O₇²⁻?
cards.back: +6 for each chromium atom.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write the oxidation half-equation for iodide to iodine.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write the reduction half-equation for chlorine.
cards.back: Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write the oxidation half-equation for magnesium.
cards.back: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write the reduction half-equation Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺.
cards.back: Fe³⁺ + e⁻ → Fe²⁺.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How do you balance oxygen in an acidic half-equation?
cards.back: Add H₂O to the side needing oxygen.
accept: Add H₂O to the side needing oxygen.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How do you balance hydrogen in an acidic half-equation?
cards.back: Add H⁺ to the side needing hydrogen.
accept: Add H⁺ to the side needing hydrogen.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write the acidic reduction half-equation for MnO₄⁻ → Mn²⁺.
cards.back: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write the acidic reduction half-equation for dichromate(VI).
cards.back: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: When equalising electrons, what must you multiply?
cards.back: Every term of the entire half-equation, not electrons alone.
accept: Every term of the entire half-equation, not electrons alone.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Combine Fe³⁺ reduction with I⁻ oxidation.
cards.back: 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is periodicity?
cards.back: A repeating pattern of properties as atomic number increases.
accept: A repeating pattern of properties as atomic number increases.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What determines an element's position in the modern periodic table?
cards.back: Its atomic number (proton number).

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is helium an s-block element although placed in Group 0?
cards.back: Its electronic configuration is 1s².

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which subshell is filling from Al to Ar?
cards.back: The 3p subshell.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write sodium's electron configuration beyond [Ne].
cards.back: 3s¹.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write aluminium's electron configuration beyond [Ne].
cards.back: 3s² 3p¹.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write the first-ionisation equation for Na.
cards.back: Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which Period 3 elements have giant metallic structures?
cards.back: Sodium, magnesium and aluminium.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How many covalent bonds does each silicon atom make in its network?
cards.back: Four, in a giant covalent structure.
accept: Four, in a giant covalent structure.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What molecular formula is used for white phosphorus?
cards.back: P₄.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What molecular formula is used for the common sulfur molecule?
cards.back: S₈.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why are measured argon radii not directly like chlorine's covalent radius?
cards.back: Argon is monatomic; its quoted van der Waals radius uses a different definition.
accept: Argon is monatomic; its quoted van der Waals radius uses a different definition.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the general outer configuration of Group 2 atoms?
cards.back: ns².

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What general formula do Group 2 oxides have?
cards.back: MO, e.g. MgO.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What formula results when Mg²⁺ combines with OH⁻?
cards.back: Mg(OH)₂.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write magnesium's slow reaction with cold water.
cards.back: Mg + 2H₂O → Mg(OH)₂ + H₂.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write magnesium's reaction with steam.
cards.back: Mg + H₂O(g) → MgO + H₂.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write calcium's reaction with water.
cards.back: Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write strontium's reaction with water.
cards.back: Sr + 2H₂O → Sr(OH)₂ + H₂.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write barium's reaction with water.
cards.back: Ba + 2H₂O → Ba(OH)₂ + H₂.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What product differs for Mg reacting with steam versus cold water?
cards.back: Steam gives MgO; cold water gives Mg(OH)₂.
accept: Steam gives MgO; cold water gives Mg(OH)₂.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How do first and second ionisation energies affect Group 2 reactivity?
cards.back: Both generally decrease down the group, so losing two electrons is easier.
accept: Both generally decrease down the group, so losing two electrons is easier.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is a saturated Ba(OH)₂ solution more alkaline than Mg(OH)₂?
cards.back: More Ba(OH)₂ dissolves, giving a higher OH⁻ concentration.
accept: More Ba(OH)₂ dissolves, giving a higher OH⁻ concentration.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write the neutralisation of Mg(OH)₂ by HCl.
cards.back: Mg(OH)₂ + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + 2H₂O.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write calcium hydroxide neutralising H⁺ in acidic soil.
cards.back: Ca(OH)₂ + 2H⁺ → Ca²⁺ + 2H₂O.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write the reaction extracting titanium using magnesium.
cards.back: TiCl₄ + 2Mg → Ti + 2MgCl₂.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What are the titanium oxidation states before and after extraction?
cards.back: +4 in TiCl₄; 0 in Ti metal.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write calcium oxide removing sulfur dioxide.
cards.back: CaO + SO₂ → CaSO₃.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can BaSO₄ be used in medical imaging?
cards.back: Very insoluble, so little Ba²⁺ is released; also absorbs X-rays.
accept: Very insoluble, so little Ba²⁺ is released; also absorbs X-rays.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write the net ionic equation for the sulfate ion test.
cards.back: Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄(s), a white precipitate.
accept: Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄(s), a white precipitate.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why should you not acidify the sulfate test using H₂SO₄?
cards.back: It introduces sulfate and can give a false positive.
accept: It introduces sulfate and can give a false positive.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the general outer configuration of halogens?
cards.back: ns²np⁵.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the formula of a halogen molecule?
cards.back: X₂: e.g. F₂, Cl₂, Br₂ or I₂.
accept: X₂: e.g. F₂, Cl₂, Br₂ or I₂.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the colour and state of fluorine at room temperature?
cards.back: Pale yellow gas.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is aqueous silver fluoride not a halide-test precipitate?
cards.back: AgF is soluble in water.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which is the strongest oxidising halogen?
cards.back: Fluorine, F₂.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write chlorine displacing bromide ions.
cards.back: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write chlorine displacing iodide ions.
cards.back: Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write bromine displacing iodide ions.
cards.back: Br₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Br⁻ + I₂.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: In Cl₂ + 2Br⁻, which is the oxidising agent?
cards.back: Cl₂, because it is reduced from 0 to −1.
accept: Cl₂, because it is reduced from 0 to −1.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write NaCl reacting with concentrated H₂SO₄ (acid–base only).
cards.back: NaCl + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HCl.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write the redox equation for HBr reducing sulfuric acid.
cards.back: 2HBr + H₂SO₄ → Br₂ + SO₂ + 2H₂O.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What sulfur-containing products can iodide form from H₂SO₄?
cards.back: SO₂, elemental sulfur and H₂S.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is sulfur's oxidation state in H₂S?

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why use nitric, not hydrochloric, acid in a silver-halide test?
cards.back: HCl introduces chloride ions and could give a false AgCl precipitate.
accept: HCl introduces chloride ions and could give a false AgCl precipitate.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write the ionic equation for a silver bromide precipitate.
cards.back: Ag⁺ + Br⁻ → AgBr(s), a cream precipitate.
accept: Ag⁺ + Br⁻ → AgBr(s), a cream precipitate.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which soluble complex helps silver chloride dissolve in NH₃?
cards.back: [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write chlorine reacting reversibly with water.
cards.back: Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens to Cl oxidation states in chlorine-water disproportionation?
cards.back: 0 in Cl₂ becomes −1 in HCl and +1 in HClO.
accept: 0 in Cl₂ becomes −1 in HCl and +1 in HClO.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write chlorine-water's oxygen-forming overall equation.
cards.back: 2Cl₂ + 2H₂O → 4HCl + O₂.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Write chlorine reacting with cold, dilute NaOH.
cards.back: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is chlorate(I)'s formula and Cl oxidation state?
cards.back: ClO⁻, with chlorine +1.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which oxyanion is chlorate(V), not chlorate(I)?
cards.back: ClO₃⁻, with chlorine +5.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is chlorination used despite possible by-products?
cards.back: It prevents waterborne infections; treatment is controlled and monitored.
accept: It prevents waterborne infections; treatment is controlled and monitored.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: A white silver-halide precipitate soluble in dilute ammonia indicates which halide?
cards.back: Chloride, Cl⁻.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: A cream silver-halide precipitate soluble only in concentrated ammonia indicates?
cards.back: Bromide, Br⁻.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: A yellow silver-halide precipitate insoluble in ammonia indicates which ion?
cards.back: Iodide, I⁻.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which anion gives a white barium sulfate precipitate in a confirmed ion test?
cards.back: Sulfate, SO₄²⁻.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which anion is suggested by bubbles of CO₂ in a carbonate identification test?
cards.back: Carbonate, CO₃²⁻.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which gas turns limewater cloudy in a carbonate test?
cards.back: Carbon dioxide, CO₂.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which ion is indicated when a sample gives ammonia in a qualitative ion test?
cards.back: Ammonium, NH₄⁺.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the diagnostic effect of ammonia gas on damp red litmus?
cards.back: It turns blue.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What observation supports the presence of hydroxide ions in a water sample?
cards.back: An alkaline indicator response.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: In a test result, what does effervescence mean?
cards.back: Visible bubbles of gas being produced.
accept: Visible bubbles of gas being produced.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is a white precipitate alone not proof of sulfate?
cards.back: Another insoluble salt may give a similar observation.
accept: Another insoluble salt may give a similar observation.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why compare both precipitate colour and solubility in halide analysis?
cards.back: Together they distinguish similar silver halides.
accept: Together they distinguish similar silver halides.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the formula of the insoluble solid confirming sulfate with Ba²⁺?
cards.back: BaSO₄.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can a confirmation observation matter after a first precipitate forms?
cards.back: A first result may be shared by different ions.
accept: A first result may be shared by different ions.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Bromine water changes from orange to colourless in a functional-group test. What bond is suggested?
cards.back: A carbon–carbon double bond, C=C.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does unchanged orange bromine water suggest about an unknown sample?
cards.back: No positive evidence for C=C unsaturation in that test.
accept: No positive evidence for C=C unsaturation in that test.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does an orange-to-colourless result not uniquely identify one organic molecule?
cards.back: Different compounds can give the same observation.
accept: Different compounds can give the same observation.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: A positive carbonate–acid identification gives which observable sign?
cards.back: Bubbles of carbon dioxide.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What class of organic compounds commonly gives CO₂ in a carbonate test?
cards.back: Carboxylic acids.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What distinguishes a compound with –COOH from an alcohol with –OH?
cards.back: Carboxylic acids have an acidic carbonyl-containing group.
accept: Carboxylic acids have an acidic carbonyl-containing group.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What extra structural feature distinguishes –COOH from an alcohol –OH group?
cards.back: An adjacent carbonyl group, C=O.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Can the orange-to-green oxidation observation alone distinguish primary from secondary alcohols?
cards.back: No; both types can be oxidised.
accept: No; both types can be oxidised.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is no orange-to-green change consistent with a tertiary alcohol?
cards.back: Tertiary alcohols resist oxidation under standard test conditions.
accept: Tertiary alcohols resist oxidation under standard test conditions.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What extra evidence can distinguish an aldehyde from a ketone?
cards.back: A positive Tollens’ or Fehling’s result indicates an aldehyde.
accept: A positive Tollens’ or Fehling’s result indicates an aldehyde.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: An orange 2,4-DNPH precipitate and no Tollens silver deposit suggest what?
cards.back: A ketone.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: An orange 2,4-DNPH precipitate and a positive Tollens result suggest what?
cards.back: An aldehyde.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What group is supported by an orange 2,4-DNPH precipitate?
cards.back: Aldehyde or ketone carbonyl.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does 2,4-DNPH not distinguish aldehydes from ketones?
cards.back: Both functional groups give a positive result.
accept: Both functional groups give a positive result.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What result is expected for a ketone in a valid Tollens’ test?
cards.back: No silver mirror or silver deposit.
accept: No silver mirror or silver deposit.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What result is expected for a ketone in a valid Fehling’s test?
cards.back: No brick-red precipitate.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens to silver ions in a positive Tollens’ result?
cards.back: They are reduced to metallic silver.
accept: They are reduced to metallic silver.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens to copper(II) ions in a positive Fehling’s result?
cards.back: They form red copper(I) oxide.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which two tests help distinguish an aldehyde from a ketone?
cards.back: Tollens’ and Fehling’s.
accept: silver mirror and brick red tests

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: An IR spectrum shows C=O near 1700 cm⁻¹ and very broad O–H. What group is likely?
cards.back: Carboxylic acid.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Where is the very broad carboxylic-acid O–H band approximately?

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Can an IR carbonyl band alone distinguish an aldehyde from a ketone?
cards.back: No; both contain C=O.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: A broad alcohol O–H band without C=O suggests which group?
cards.back: An alcohol.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does an IR fingerprint match help identify a compound?
cards.back: Its detailed absorption pattern can be distinctive.
accept: Its detailed absorption pattern can be distinctive.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does an absent characteristic absorption suggest in IR analysis?
cards.back: The corresponding bond or group may be absent.
accept: The corresponding bond or group may be absent.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is one positive functional-group test insufficient for an exact identity?
cards.back: Many molecules share that functional group.
accept: Many molecules share that functional group.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: In a halogenoalkane hydrolysis comparison, what does faster silver-halide formation indicate?
cards.back: Faster release of halide ions.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can silver-halide appearance be used as evidence of hydrolysis?
cards.back: Hydrolysis releases halide ions into solution.
accept: Hydrolysis releases halide ions into solution.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which bond usually hydrolyses faster in comparable haloalkanes: C–Cl or C–I?
cards.back: C–I.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: A green hydroxide precipitate in an aqueous metal-ion test suggests which ion?
cards.back: Fe²⁺.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: A brown hydroxide precipitate in an aqueous metal-ion test suggests which ion?
cards.back: Fe³⁺.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: A blue hydroxide precipitate in an aqueous metal-ion test suggests which ion?
cards.back: Cu²⁺.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: A white hydroxide precipitate that can redissolve as hydroxoaluminate suggests?
cards.back: Al³⁺.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is the colour of a precipitate useful but not always conclusive?
cards.back: Different substances can produce similar colours.
accept: Different substances can produce similar colours.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which two aqueous iron oxidation states can be separated by green versus brown precipitates?
cards.back: Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a deep-blue copper(II) solution signal in ligand-identification questions?
cards.back: An ammine complex of Cu²⁺.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does amphoteric mean for a metal hydroxide?
cards.back: It reacts with both acids and bases.
accept: It reacts with both acids and bases.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can colour change without a metal-ion oxidation-state change?
cards.back: A change of ligand alters d-orbital splitting.
accept: A change of ligand alters d-orbital splitting.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a concordant titre mean?
cards.back: A titre close to other valid repeat results.
accept: A titre close to other valid repeat results.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the titration end point?
cards.back: The observed indicator colour change.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How does the end point differ from the equivalence point?
cards.back: End point is observed; equivalence is stoichiometric.
accept: End point is observed; equivalence is stoichiometric.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does the equivalence point mean in a titration?
cards.back: Reactants have combined in their stoichiometric ratio.
accept: Reactants have combined in their stoichiometric ratio.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can a colour change at the end point differ from exact equivalence?
cards.back: The indicator changes over a pH range.
accept: The indicator changes over a pH range.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is an anomalous titre?
cards.back: One inconsistent with the other valid titres.
accept: One inconsistent with the other valid titres.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a rough titre help establish in data analysis?
cards.back: The approximate equivalence volume.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why are concordant titres averaged instead of all titres uncritically?
cards.back: It reduces random error without including clear anomalies.
accept: It reduces random error without including clear anomalies.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a false positive in a chemical identification test?
cards.back: A positive result when the target substance is absent.
accept: A positive result when the target substance is absent.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a false negative in an identification test?
cards.back: A negative result when the target substance is present.
accept: A negative result when the target substance is present.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a confirmatory test in qualitative analysis?
cards.back: Another observation supporting the proposed identity.
accept: Another observation supporting the proposed identity.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a qualitative result?
cards.back: A description of a property, not a numerical measurement.
accept: A description of a property, not a numerical measurement.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a quantitative result?
cards.back: A numerical measurement with units where appropriate.
accept: A numerical measurement with units where appropriate.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why must an observation be distinguished from an inference?
cards.back: An observation is seen; an inference interprets its cause.
accept: An observation is seen; an inference interprets its cause.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the dependent variable in a practical?
cards.back: The quantity measured as conditions change.
accept: The quantity measured as conditions change.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a control variable?
cards.back: A factor kept constant for a fair comparison.
accept: A factor kept constant for a fair comparison.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the standard molar entropy S° of a substance?
cards.back: Entropy per mole in its standard state at a stated temperature.
accept: Entropy per mole in its standard state at a stated temperature.
entropy of one mole in standard state

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the enthalpy of solution?
cards.back: Enthalpy change when one mole of solute forms an infinitely dilute aqueous solution.
accept: Enthalpy change when one mole of solute forms an infinitely dilute aqueous solution.
Enthalpy change when one mole of solute dissolves to form solution.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a Born–Haber cycle?
cards.back: An enthalpy cycle linking ionic lattice formation to other steps.
accept: An enthalpy cycle linking ionic lattice formation to other steps.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why are standard enthalpy quantities per mole?
cards.back: The defined change is for one mole of the specified process.
accept: The defined change is for one mole of the specified process.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a half-cell in electrochemistry?
cards.back: One redox couple forming an electrode system.
accept: One redox couple forming an electrode system.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does standard electrode potential compare?
cards.back: A half-cell potential against the standard hydrogen electrode.
accept: A half-cell potential against the standard hydrogen electrode.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the sign of a more positive standard electrode potential linked to?
cards.back: Greater tendency for reduction under standard conditions.
accept: Greater tendency for reduction under standard conditions.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is a cell potential not automatically its operating voltage?
cards.back: Non-standard conditions and internal losses can change it.
accept: Non-standard conditions and internal losses can change it.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is repeatability in measurement?
cards.back: Agreement when the same person repeats a method using the same equipment.
accept: Agreement when the same person repeats a method using the same equipment.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is reproducibility in measurement?
cards.back: Agreement when conditions such as observer or equipment change.
accept: Agreement when conditions such as observer or equipment change.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is measurement resolution?
cards.back: The smallest distinguishable change shown by an instrument.
accept: The smallest distinguishable change shown by an instrument.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does fractional uncertainty mean?
cards.back: Absolute uncertainty divided by the measured value.
accept: Absolute uncertainty divided by the measured value.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why does a high-resolution instrument not guarantee accuracy?
cards.back: It may still have systematic error.
accept: It may still have systematic error.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does an order-of-magnitude estimate communicate?
cards.back: An approximate power of ten.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the difference between stiffness and Young modulus?
cards.back: Stiffness depends on dimensions; Young modulus is a material property.
accept: Stiffness depends on dimensions; Young modulus is a material property.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is elastic deformation?
cards.back: Deformation that reverses when the load is removed.
accept: Deformation that reverses when the load is removed.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why is stress different from force?
cards.back: Stress is force per unit cross-sectional area.
accept: Stress is force per unit cross-sectional area.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why is strain dimensionless?
cards.back: It is a ratio of extension to original length.
accept: It is a ratio of extension to original length.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is wave intensity?
cards.back: Power transmitted per unit area.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What happens to wave intensity if amplitude doubles?
cards.back: It quadruples, under otherwise identical conditions.
accept: It quadruples, under otherwise identical conditions.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does a coherent pair of sources maintain?
cards.back: A constant phase difference and the same frequency.
accept: A constant phase difference and the same frequency.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does the gradient at the start of a product–time curve give?
cards.back: Initial rate of product formation.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is a tangent needed on a curved rate graph?
cards.back: The gradient changes with time.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a rate graph's horizontal section show?
cards.back: The measured quantity has stopped changing.
accept: The measured quantity has stopped changing.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a shorter time to a fixed reaction endpoint suggest?
cards.back: A faster mean reaction rate.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does an initial-rate comparison deliberately minimise?
cards.back: Changes in reactant concentrations during the reading.
accept: Changes in reactant concentrations during the reading.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: In rate experiments, what does a clock endpoint represent?
cards.back: The same chosen extent of change each time.
accept: The same chosen extent of change each time.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: For otherwise comparable clock reactions, rate is approximately proportional to?
cards.back: 1 divided by the endpoint time.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can 1/time be only an approximate rate measure?
cards.back: It relies on reaching an equivalent endpoint each run.
accept: It relies on reaching an equivalent endpoint each run.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How does measuring a tangent avoid an average-rate result?
cards.back: It estimates rate at one particular instant.
accept: It estimates rate at one particular instant.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does the horizontal axis normally show on an acid–base titration curve?
cards.back: Volume of titrant added.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does the vertical axis show on a titration curve?
cards.back: pH.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is the equivalence point not always pH 7?
cards.back: The reacting acid and base may have different strengths.
accept: The reacting acid and base may have different strengths.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Where is the buffer region on a weak-acid titration curve?
cards.back: Before equivalence, where both acid and conjugate base are present.
accept: Before equivalence, where both acid and conjugate base are present.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a shallow pH-curve section generally mean?
cards.back: pH changes slowly with added titrant.
accept: pH changes slowly with added titrant.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can the starting pH differ for equal-concentration weak and strong acids?
cards.back: The weak acid only partially ionises.
accept: The weak acid only partially ionises.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What quantity locates the equivalence point on the horizontal scale?
cards.back: Volume of titrant at equivalence.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a pH curve's steep region help select?
cards.back: An indicator with a suitable transition range.
accept: An indicator with a suitable transition range.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a limitation of using a single indicator colour to draw a full pH curve?
cards.back: It does not give continuous numerical pH data.
accept: It does not give continuous numerical pH data.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a positive measured cell emf show for the cell as written?
cards.back: The stated overall cell reaction is feasible under the conditions.
accept: The stated overall cell reaction is feasible under the conditions.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does the salt bridge supply to the circuit?
cards.back: A path for charge balance by ion movement.
accept: A path for charge balance by ion movement.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens to cell emf if ion concentrations change?
cards.back: It can differ from the standard emf.
accept: It can differ from the standard emf.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does the superscript ° in E°cell signify?
cards.back: Standard conditions.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which half-cell undergoes oxidation in a galvanic cell?
cards.back: The anode.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which half-cell undergoes reduction in a galvanic cell?
cards.back: The cathode.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why must an electrode potential be quoted relative to a reference?
cards.back: A single absolute electrode potential is not directly measured.
accept: A single absolute electrode potential is not directly measured.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What can a narrow melting range suggest for an organic solid?
cards.back: Higher purity.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How can impurities alter the melting point of an organic solid?
cards.back: They usually lower and broaden its melting range.
accept: They usually lower and broaden its melting range.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can a boiling point help assess liquid purity?
cards.back: A pure liquid has a characteristic value at stated pressure.
accept: A pure liquid has a characteristic value at stated pressure.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How does pressure affect the use of boiling point as an identity test?
cards.back: Boiling point depends on pressure.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is recrystallisation intended to improve?
cards.back: Purity of a solid product.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What distinguishes percentage purity from percentage yield?
cards.back: Purity is desired substance in sample; yield is actual versus theoretical product.
accept: Purity is desired substance in sample; yield is actual versus theoretical product.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why must a melting point be compared with a reference?
cards.back: It supports identity and purity assessment.
accept: It supports identity and purity assessment.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a spot's Rf value compare?
cards.back: Distance travelled by spot divided by solvent-front distance.
accept: Distance travelled by spot divided by solvent-front distance.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does one matching Rf not prove a unique identity?
cards.back: Different substances may have similar Rf values.
accept: Different substances may have similar Rf values.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What can two separated spots reveal about a sample?
cards.back: It contains at least two detectable components.
accept: It contains at least two detectable components.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does a single TLC spot fail to prove conclusively?
cards.back: That the sample contains only one compound.
accept: That the sample contains only one compound.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why should chromatograms be compared under similar conditions?
cards.back: Rf depends on the solvent and stationary phase.
accept: Rf depends on the solvent and stationary phase.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which phase remains in place in TLC?
cards.back: The stationary phase.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which phase carries substances along in chromatography?
cards.back: The mobile phase.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What property most directly determines how far a TLC spot travels?
cards.back: Relative attraction to stationary and mobile phases.
accept: Relative attraction to stationary and mobile phases.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why might excess ligand change a complex ion's observed colour?
cards.back: It changes the d-orbital splitting.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a hexaaqua complex?
cards.back: A metal ion surrounded by six water ligands.
accept: A metal ion surrounded by six water ligands.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a functional-group test?
cards.back: An observation used to infer a characteristic group.
accept: An observation used to infer a characteristic group.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is qualitative chemical analysis?
cards.back: Identifying substances or properties without measuring their amount.
accept: Identifying substances or properties without measuring their amount.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a confirmatory observation?
cards.back: Additional evidence supporting a proposed identity.
accept: Additional evidence supporting a proposed identity.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is an analytical reference standard?
cards.back: A known material used for comparison.
accept: A known material used for comparison.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can an IR spectrum confirm an identity more securely than one peak?
cards.back: Multiple absorption features form a distinctive pattern.
accept: Multiple absorption features form a distinctive pattern.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the rate constant?
cards.back: The proportionality constant in the rate equation at a fixed temperature.
accept: The proportionality constant in the rate equation at a fixed temperature.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does equilibrium position describe?
cards.back: Relative amounts of reactants and products at equilibrium.
accept: Relative amounts of reactants and products at equilibrium.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the difference between random uncertainty and a systematic offset?
cards.back: Random causes scatter; systematic shifts measurements consistently.
accept: Random causes scatter; systematic shifts measurements consistently.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does calibration check?
cards.back: Readings against known reference values.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does a maximum-gradient line represent?
cards.back: A steep plausible straight line consistent with the data.
accept: A steep plausible straight line consistent with the data.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does a minimum-gradient line represent?
cards.back: A shallow plausible straight line consistent with the data.
accept: A shallow plausible straight line consistent with the data.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is internal resistance?
cards.back: Resistance within a source that causes voltage loss under current.
accept: Resistance within a source that causes voltage loss under current.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why can terminal p.d. be less than emf?
cards.back: Some energy per charge is lost across internal resistance.
accept: Some energy per charge is lost across internal resistance.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why does wire diameter matter greatly to a resistivity result?
cards.back: Cross-sectional area scales with diameter squared.
accept: Cross-sectional area scales with diameter squared.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why must the cladding of an optical fibre have a lower refractive index than its core?
cards.back: To allow total internal reflection at the core–cladding boundary.
accept: To allow total internal reflection at the core–cladding boundary.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is material dispersion in an optical fibre?
cards.back: Pulse spreading because different wavelengths travel at different speeds.
accept: Pulse spreading because different wavelengths travel at different speeds.
different wavelengths travel at different speeds

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is modal dispersion in a step-index optical fibre?
cards.back: Pulse spreading because light travels along different paths of different lengths.
accept: Pulse spreading because light travels along different paths of different lengths.
different modes have different travel times

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why can pulse broadening reduce an optical fibre's maximum data rate?
cards.back: Adjacent light pulses may overlap and become hard to distinguish.
accept: Adjacent light pulses may overlap and become hard to distinguish.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does attenuation mean for light travelling along an optical fibre?
cards.back: A reduction in the optical signal's power or intensity.
accept: A reduction in the optical signal's power or intensity.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What source property helps reduce material dispersion?
cards.back: A narrow range of wavelengths.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Which type of optical fibre greatly reduces modal dispersion?
cards.back: Single-mode optical fibre.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Define a zwitterion.
cards.back: An ion with both positive and negative charges but no overall charge.
accept: An ion with both positive and negative charges but no overall charge.
both positive and negative charges with net zero
no net charge but both charges

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What form does a simple amino acid predominantly take in strongly acidic solution?
cards.back: A positive ion with –NH₃⁺ and –COOH groups.
accept: A positive ion with –NH₃⁺ and –COOH groups.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What form does a simple amino acid predominantly take in strongly alkaline solution?
cards.back: A negative ion with –NH₂ and –COO⁻ groups.
accept: A negative ion with –NH₂ and –COO⁻ groups.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which amino-acid functional group accepts a proton and acts as a base?
cards.back: The amine group, –NH₂.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which amino-acid functional group donates a proton and acts as an acid?
cards.back: The carboxylic acid group, –COOH.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is produced when all the peptide bonds in a protein are hydrolysed?
cards.back: Its constituent amino acids.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What type of bonds join successive nucleotides within one DNA strand?
cards.back: Covalent bonds in the sugar–phosphate backbone.
accept: Covalent bonds in the sugar–phosphate backbone.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How many hydrogen bonds link adenine and thymine in DNA?
cards.back: Two hydrogen bonds.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How many hydrogen bonds link cytosine and guanine in DNA?
cards.back: Three hydrogen bonds.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does denaturation often stop an enzyme binding its substrate?
cards.back: Its active site changes shape.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which levels of protein structure may denaturation disrupt without breaking peptide bonds?
cards.back: Secondary and tertiary structure.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Define coordination number in a metal complex.
cards.back: The number of coordinate bonds to its central metal ion.
accept: The number of coordinate bonds to its central metal ion.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: If d-orbital energy splitting increases, what happens to the absorbed light's wavelength?
cards.back: It decreases.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why are heterogeneous catalysts often spread over a support material?
cards.back: To increase available active surface area while using less catalyst.
accept: To increase available active surface area while using less catalyst.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a catalytic intermediate in homogeneous catalysis?
cards.back: A temporary species formed with the catalyst and used up later in the cycle.
accept: A temporary species formed with the catalyst and used up later in the cycle.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which ion acts as an autocatalyst in the manganate(VII)–ethanedioate reaction?
cards.back: Mn²⁺, manganese(II) ions.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the mobile phase in gas chromatography?
cards.back: A carrier gas.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What can form the stationary phase in gas chromatography?
cards.back: A solid or a non-volatile liquid coating a solid.
accept: A solid or a non-volatile liquid coating a solid.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Define retention time in gas chromatography.
cards.back: The time between sample injection and detection of a component.
accept: The time between sample injection and detection of a component.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the mobile phase in column chromatography?
cards.back: A liquid solvent.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the SI base unit for thermodynamic temperature?
cards.back: kelvin (K)

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Which prefix represents 10⁻¹⁵?
cards.back: femto (f)

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Which prefix represents 10¹²?
cards.back: tera (T)

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What quantity has base units kg m² s⁻³?
cards.back: Power.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does an uncertainty error bar represent?
cards.back: A range of plausible values for the measured quantity.
accept: A range of plausible values for the measured quantity.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Which graph lines estimate uncertainty in a straight-line gradient?
cards.back: The steepest and shallowest acceptable lines.
accept: The steepest and shallowest acceptable lines.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Which uncertainty type cannot be removed by repeated readings alone?
cards.back: Systematic uncertainty.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why quote an uncertainty to an appropriate number of significant figures?
cards.back: Extra digits imply unjustified precision.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does reproducibility require beyond repeatability?
cards.back: Different investigators or apparatus under changed conditions.
accept: Different investigators or apparatus under changed conditions.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does the strong nuclear force do at very short separations below about 0.5 fm?
cards.back: It becomes repulsive.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the approximate maximum range of the attractive strong nuclear force?
cards.back: About 3 femtometres.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What conservation argument led to the prediction of the neutrino?
